10309.s: This order returns possession, use, and control of two tracts of land from the Fort Armstrong Military Reservation to the Territory of Hawaii and transfers title to those lands. It says the land is needed for a harbor-improvement project. Before the transfer, Hawaii must replace or move certain Army-related facilities and utility lines, and it must pay the costs for that work.

10308.s: This order says federal contracting agencies are mainly responsible for making contractors and subcontractors follow nondiscrimination rules in contracts. It sets up the Committee on Government Contract Compliance to study how the rules are carried out and to make recommendations to prevent or end discrimination. It also directs government contracting agencies to cooperate with the committee and provide information and help as allowed by law.

10307.s: This order gives the Secretary of State the President’s authority to set rules for how consular officers execute and return commissions in certain cases. It also lets the Secretary set fee schedules for witnesses, foreign counsel, and interpreters, and make those rules apply to diplomatic officers. The order revokes a 1939 executive order on the same subject.

10306.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate disputes between the Akron & Barberton Belt Railroad Company, other listed carriers, and certain workers represented by listed railway labor organizations. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. It also says the board must follow section 502 of the Defense Production Act and does not change the Secretary of the Army’s authority under Executive Order 10155.

10305.s: This order revokes Executive Order No. 10207, which had created the President's Commission on Internal Security and Individual Rights. It also directs the Department of the Treasury to liquidate the Commission's remaining affairs and use any unspent funds for that purpose.

10304.s: This order makes certain income, excess-profits, declared value excess-profits, capital stock, estate, and gift tax returns for periods up to 1950 open to inspection by the Senate Committee on Armed Services or an authorized subcommittee. The inspection is for studying policies, programs, activities, operations, facilities, requirements, and practices of the Department of Defense, the Armed Services, and other agencies that carry out related functions.

10303.s: The order creates a three-member board to investigate a labor dispute between several railroad carriers operated under Federal management and certain of their employees represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen and Enginemen. The board is directed to report its findings to the President within 30 days. The order also says it does not change the authority of the Secretary of the Army over the transportation systems under Executive Order 10155.

10302.s: This order creates the Interdepartmental Committee on Narcotics and gives it members from several federal departments and the Federal Security Agency. The committee is to collect and share information about illegal sales and use of narcotic drugs and marihuana, drug addiction, and the laws and conventions tied to them. It is also to study prevention, control, treatment, and rehabilitation, and advise the President. Federal departments and agencies are asked to cooperate and provide information.

10301.s: This order changes the rules for the Wage Stabilization Board by adding up to six alternate members. The President may appoint these alternate members, and no more than two may represent the public, two labor, and two business and industry. Alternate members may serve only when a regular member is not taking part and only when the Chairman calls on them to do so.

10299.s: This order adds the Bonneville Power Administration as an agency covered under Title I of the Renegotiation Act of 1951. It says the law applies to all contracts with the Bonneville Power Administration and related subcontracts for amounts received or accrued on or after November 1, 1951. This affects the agency and the contractors and subcontractors that work with it.

10300.s: This order gives the Director for Mutual Security many of the President’s duties under the Mutual Security Act of 1951 and related laws. It also puts international development programs under the Director’s coordination, direction, and supervision, and says the Secretary of Defense must work under that same oversight for certain duties. The order provides for transferring some personnel, records, property, and funds to the Director, and it revokes some prior orders and related actions.

10297.s: This order creates a Telecommunications Advisor to the President in the Executive Office of the President, to be appointed by the President. The advisor helps coordinate telecommunications policies and standards for the executive branch, manage telecommunications planning and programs, and develop government frequency requirements. The advisor also assigns radio frequencies to government agencies and works with the Federal Communications Commission and other agencies.

10298.s: This order extends Part I of Executive Order 10210 to the Department of the Interior. It authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to carry out the functions and authority given in that part, subject to its limits and regulations. The Secretary’s regulations do not need approval from the Secretary of Defense, and the order does not affect any other procurement authority the department may have.

10295.s: This order approves a seal as the official seal of the United States Court of Military Appeals. The seal shows a sword, a balance with scales, oak leaves, and the court’s name on a dark blue band.

10296.s: This order gives certain defense housing and community facilities functions to the Director of Defense Mobilization, the Defense Production Administrator, the Housing and Home Finance Administrator, and the Federal Security Administrator. It covers things like finding critical defense-housing areas, defining defense installations, suspending residential credit restrictions, and handling some community facilities and services for recreation, child day-care centers, and libraries. It also requires consultation or approval from other officials on roads, territorial programs, public health, water supply, sewerage, and some construction work.

10294.s: This order designates the Defense Materials Procurement Agency, the Bureau of Mines, and the United States Geological Survey as agencies included in the term "Department" for Title I of the Renegotiation Act of 1951. It makes Title I apply to their contracts and related subcontracts, to the extent of amounts received or accrued on or after October 1, 1951, even if the contracts were made before that date.

10293.s: This order amends how powers under Title I of the Housing and Rent Act of 1947 are handled. It says those powers are to be administered through the Economic Stabilization Agency and may be carried out by the Economic Stabilization Administrator or other officers and agencies he designates. It also says exceptions for people engaged in national defense activities must be handled in consultation with the Housing and Home Finance Administrator or his representative.

10292.s: This order changes the Selective Service rules under the Universal Military Training and Service Act. It updates definitions, the duties of Selective Service officers, and how board areas are set up, including special rules for New York City. It also says which male citizens and other male persons must register, which persons are exempt, and when some people must register after leaving the armed forces, entering the United States, or leaving an institution.

10291.s: This order reserves the airspace above a specified area in Georgia and South Carolina for national defense and other governmental purposes. No one may navigate an aircraft in that airspace except by authority of the United States Atomic Energy Commission. People who violate the order are subject to penalties under the Civil Aeronautics Act of 1938. It became effective on October 3, 1951.

10289.s: This order lets the Secretary of the Treasury perform several presidential functions without further approval. It covers customs districts, anti-smuggling actions, vessel rules, gold and silver regulations, and some tax district matters. It also lets the Secretary of the Treasury and the Postmaster General set rules for shipping valuables by federal departments and employees.

10290.s: This order sets minimum standards for how executive branch departments and agencies classify, send, and handle official information that must be protected for national security. It creates four security categories: "Top Secret," "Secret," "Confidential," and "Restricted," and says only information that needs this protection may be classified. It also says agency heads and other executive branch personnel are responsible for following and carrying out these safeguards.

10287.s: This order revokes Executive Order No. 8034 of January 14, 1939. It also abolishes the Federal Real Estate Board that was created by that earlier order.

10288.s: This order changes the rules for some federal employees to acquire a competitive status. It says an employee must have served continuously in full-time, active-duty status in the competitive service during the two years before the order, with military service not counted as a break in service. It also says the agency head must recommend the employee within six months, with special timing rules for employees who enter the armed forces and for certain postal substitute employees.

10286.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Pullman Company and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. For that time, and for thirty days after the report, the company and its employees may not make changes in the conditions that led to the dispute except by agreement.

10284.s: This order extends several deadlines under a housing law about temporary housing and housing projects. It gives more time to file requests, meet transfer or relinquishment conditions, notify tenants to vacate, and start eviction actions. It also extends deadlines for municipalities or counties to request conveyance of housing projects, show a need for low-rent housing, and sign required cooperation agreements.

10285.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Denver & Rio Grande Western Railroad Company, including the Denver & Salt Lake Railroad Company, and certain workers represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers. The dispute is between a carrier under Federal management and certain workers, and it has not been adjusted under the Railway Labor Act. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days and must follow section 502 of the Defense Production Act of 1950.

10283.s: This order creates a Board of Inquiry to look into labor disputes in the copper and other non-ferrous metals industry. The disputes involve certain employers and employees represented by labor organizations, including the International Union of Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers, several Railroad Brotherhoods, and unions affiliated with the American Federation of Labor. The Board must report to the President and then continue to do other duties under the law until the President ends it.

10281.s: This order creates the Defense Materials Procurement Agency and a Defense Materials Procurement Administrator. It gives the agency power to buy metals, minerals, and other materials for government use or resale, encourage mining and development of critical minerals and metals, and make subsidy payments. It also lets certain government lenders make loans to private business enterprises for expanding production and developing essential materials, including some work in foreign countries. The order transfers some personnel, records, property, and funds to the new agency and makes its work subject to direction from the Director of Defense Mobilization.

10282.s: This order suspends the eight-hour limit for laborers and mechanics employed by the Department of the Interior on public work that is designated as essential to the defense program. It applies during the national emergency and covers work done under that department. Wages are to be figured on an eight-hour day, with overtime paid at time and one-half for hours over eight in a day. It also supersedes two earlier executive orders on this subject.

10280.s: This order changes rules for commissioned officers and employees of the Public Health Service. It says the loyalty of commissioned officers can be investigated and reviewed under the federal loyalty program rules. If the Administrator finds a reasonable doubt about an officer’s loyalty to the United States Government, that officer must be separated from the Service.

10279.s: This order changes earlier rules so the Senate Special Committee to Investigate Crime in Interstate Commerce may inspect certain tax returns for any period up to and including 1950. It covers income, excess-profits, declared value excess-profits, capital stock, estate, and gift tax returns, and the inspection is subject to the stated Treasury conditions.

10278.s: This order withdraws phosphate reserved to the United States in certain patented lands in Florida from appropriation under the mineral-leasing laws. It transfers the use, possession, and control of that phosphate to the Tennessee Valley Authority for its fertilizer research and development program. The order applies subject to valid existing rights.

10277.s: This order changes rules for the security of vessels, harbors, ports, and waterfront facilities. It gives the Commandant and the captain of the port more authority over enforcement, safety conditions, and the use of security cards and other credentials. It also says masters, owners, operators, and agents remain responsible for protecting their vessels and waterfront facilities.

10276.s: This order moves certain housing and rent powers under the Housing and Rent Act of 1947 to the Economic Stabilization Agency and the Housing and Home Finance Agency. It ends the Office of the Housing Expediter and transfers its records, property, personnel, and remaining funds to those agencies. It also keeps confidential records protected and allows the Economic Stabilization Administrator to handle civil court cases related to the powers moved under the order.

10275.s: This order opens certain income, excess-profits, declared value excess-profits, capital stock, estate, and gift tax returns from 1945 to 1950 to inspection by the Senate Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments, or its authorized subcommittee. The inspection is for investigating the sale of tanker ships by the United States Maritime Commission as part of a study of government activities. The committee must follow the conditions stated in the related Treasury decision.

10274.s: This order further amends the rules for paying travel and transportation expenses for civilian officers and employees of the United States when they are transferred from one official station to another for permanent duty. It applies to shipments of household goods and personal effects that begin on or after March 5, 1951.

10272.s: This order gives the Secretary of the Army the President’s power to make rules, regulations, and restrictions for the Army and Navy hospital at Hot Springs, Arkansas. It says those rules should, as far as possible, be uniform with other hospitals under the Department of the Army. It also keeps earlier rules in effect until the Secretary of the Army changes them.

10273.s: This order exempts Herbert E. Gaston, a member of the Board of Directors of the Export-Import Bank of Washington, from compulsory retirement for age. The exemption lasts for an indefinite period, but not beyond June 30, 1955, when his current term ends.

10270.s: This order extends certain military enlistments for a period of twelve months. It applies to enlistments in the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Coast Guard that would expire after July 8, 1951, and before July 1, 1952, except for enlistments under section 4(c)(1) of the Universal Military Training and Service Act. It does not stop voluntary reenlistments or voluntary extensions under the rules of the Army, Navy, Air Force, or Coast Guard.

10271.s: This order gives the Secretary of Defense the President’s power to order members and units of Reserve components, and retired personnel of the Regular Armed Forces, into active military or naval service. It allows this service to last for up to twenty-four months, with or without their consent, and gives the Secretary of Treasury the same authority for Reserve Coast Guard components and retired Regular Coast Guard personnel.

10269.s: The order gives the Director of Defense Mobilization the President’s authority to decide which areas are critical because of national-defense activities, with respect to the need for school facilities. The Commissioner of Education must provide requested information about measures taken to provide school facilities in those areas.

10267.s: This order includes certain lands in Swain County, North Carolina, as part of the Nantahala National Forest. It approves an agreement between the Tennessee Valley Authority and the Department of Agriculture for transferring those lands. The lands are reserved for national-forest purposes under the terms of that agreement.

10268.s: This order restores certain parcels of land from the Fort Ruger Military Reservation on the Island of Oahu to the jurisdiction of the Territory of Hawaii. The order says the parcels are no longer needed for military purposes, and it includes a portion of Tract No. 1 and Tracts Nos. 2, 3, and 4 described in an earlier order.

10266.s: This order suspends some rules in the Officer Personnel Act of 1947 for Navy and Marine Corps officers in certain grades. The suspended rules deal with grade distribution, promotion by selection, temporary promotion, and discharge after a second failure to be selected for promotion. It does not suspend those promotion rules for officers already on a promotion list, and it does not suspend the discharge rule for an officer who asks to be discharged.

10264.s: This order transfers the administration of American Samoa from the Secretary of the Navy to the Secretary of the Interior. It also directs the Navy and Interior Departments, along with other executive departments and agencies, to cooperate in making the transfer. The order says the Secretary of the Interior will take needed action for civil government in American Samoa when the transfer takes effect.

10265.s: This order transfers the administration of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands from the Secretary of the Navy to the Secretary of the Interior. The Secretary of the Interior is to handle civil government there and carry out the United States' duties under the trusteeship agreement and the United Nations Charter. The President keeps the power to set security closed areas, and the Secretary of State must be kept informed on foreign policy matters.

10263.s: This order transfers the Panama Canal, related facilities, other property, records, assets, contracts, obligations, liabilities, and most personnel to the Panama Railroad Company. It does not transfer certain civil government buildings and services, the lands in the Canal Zone, or some named offices and personnel. It also revokes two earlier orders about quarters, supplies, and services related to quarters.

10262.s: This order suspends the requirement for professional examinations for promotion of medical, dental, and veterinary officers in the Regular Army and the United States Air Force. It applies during the national emergency proclaimed on December 16, 1950.

10260.s: This order designates the Federal Civil Defense Administration, the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, the Tennessee Valley Authority, and the United States Coast Guard as agencies covered under Title I of the Renegotiation Act of 1951. It also makes Title I apply to contracts and related subcontracts with those agencies for amounts received or accrued on or after July 1, 1951, even if the contracts were made before that date.

10259.s: This order gives the Secretary of State, and any Assistant Secretary of State he designates, the President’s authority under Title V of the Foreign Economic Assistance Act of 1950. That authority is for international children's welfare work.

10261.s: This order changes rules for certain Foreign Service staff officers and employees serving at posts outside the United States. It lets them receive salary differentials of up to 25 percent and gives the Secretary of State authority to designate or cancel "unhealthful" posts. It also requires related regulations and rates to be published in the Federal Register and revokes section 404 of Executive Order 10000.

10257.s: This order changes the rules for the Federal Fire Council in the General Services Administration. It says the council is an official advisory agency on protecting federal employees and property from fire, and its work is under the Administrator of General Services. It also sets the council’s governing body and revokes two earlier executive orders.

10258.s: This order changes Selective Service rules for appeals and for registrants marked delinquent. It lets a person filing an appeal ask for the case to be sent to the appeal board for the area where the registrant’s main job is located, and it requires local boards to prepare and forward the appeal record. It also requires local boards to report certain registrants who do not comply with orders to report for induction, keep records of delinquents, and send summary reports to the State Director of Selective Service.

10256.s: This order changes the rules in the Manual for Courts-Martial for some enlisted people in the military. If an enlisted person above the lowest pay grade gets a sentence with a dishonorable or bad conduct discharge, confinement, or hard labor without confinement, the sentence can reduce that person to the lowest enlisted pay grade unless regulations say otherwise. The pay after the reduction must match the person’s cumulative service.

10255.s: This order further exempts Claude L. Draper from compulsory retirement for age for five years. It applies to him as a member of the Federal Power Commission. The exemption lasts until June 22, 1956.

10253.s: This order directs the Director of the Bureau of the Budget to develop programs and issue rules for better gathering, compiling, analyzing, publishing, and sharing statistical information across executive branch agencies. It also requires a continuing study of agency statistical work and allows the Director to help agencies improve how they collect and use statistics. The order says the goals include making statistical information more reliable, timely, and comparable, while reducing the burden on people who provide the data.

10254.s: This order ends the Philippine Alien Property Administration and moves its powers, duties, property, and records to the Attorney General and the Department of Justice. It also transfers the administration’s personnel, funds, equipment, and supplies to the Department of Justice. The order says the transferred funds and property may be used for expenses tied to these functions, subject to law.

10252.s: This order makes the Canal Zone part of the Internal Revenue Collection District of Florida for all purposes allowed by U.S. internal revenue laws. It applies to the Canal Zone and takes effect on January 1, 1951.

10251.s: This order suspends the eight-hour limit for laborers and mechanics employed by the Department of Defense on public work essential to national defense during the national emergency. It says their pay will be based on an eight-hour day, with overtime paid at time and one-half for hours over eight in a day. It also supersedes earlier executive orders on this subject, but does not affect actions already taken under them.

10249.s: This order sets rules for how the Foreign Service handles requests for foreign data. It directs the Department of State to get foreign data for federal departments and agencies when requested through State. It also requires the Secretary of State to prepare standards for deciding which requests to send to the Foreign Service and how to set priorities for them.

10248.s: This order transfers listed lands from the Sacramento, California, land district to the Los Angeles, California, land district. The change is effective June 16, 1951, and affects the lands described under the Mount Diablo and San Bernardino meridians.

10250.s: This order gives the Secretary of the Interior the President’s authority to carry out many listed duties without further presidential approval. Those duties include actions about Indian agencies and tribes, land offices and land districts, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, helium, migratory birds, mineral lands, Alaska roads and tolls, and certain recreational projects. It also says earlier presidential actions on these matters stay in effect unless changed or revoked under this order.

10247.s: This order suspends the punishment limits for violations of certain articles of the Uniform Code of Military Justice. It applies to offenses committed on or after May 31, 1951, by people under the command of, or in any area controlled by, the Commander in Chief, Far East, or later commanders.

10246.s: This order transfers the use, possession, and control of the Elk River Fish Hatchery land and the improvements on it from the Department of the Interior to the Tennessee Valley Authority. The land is in Limestone County, Alabama, and it is described as about 192 acres.

10244.s: This order designates the Secretary of State and the Attorney General to handle agreements about settling intercustodial conflicts involving enemy property. It gives them powers to receive, transfer, release, or return property, interests in property, or proceeds. It also says money or property received as reimbursement by the United States will be administered by the Attorney General as vested property.

10245.s: The order creates a commission to plan an appropriate commemoration of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, by ceremonies and other means. The commission includes seven ex officio members, and federal departments and agencies are directed to cooperate with it and provide information and assistance. It ends when the commission reports that its work is completed.

10243.s: This order extends part of Executive Order 10210 to the Federal Civil Defense Administration. It lets the Federal Civil Defense Administrator use the same contract-related powers for emergency and developmental contracts, specialized contracts, contracts under authority from other federal departments or agencies, and contracts for activities approved under the Federal Civil Defense Act of 1950. The order says any regulations set by the Administrator do not need approval by the Secretary of Defense, and it does not take away any other procurement authority the Administration may have.

10242.s: The order sets rules for how the Federal Civil Defense Administrator may use part-time, temporary, voluntary, and unpaid workers under the Federal Civil Defense Act of 1950. It says these appointments should usually be limited to advisory or consultative jobs, and it requires written findings for some other appointments. It also requires public reporting of certain appointments, gives a quarterly review role to the Civil Service Commission, and limits some conflict-of-interest rules for these workers. The order also allows the Administrator to use services of Federal agencies and approves hiring retired armed services personnel under the Act.

10241.s: This order changes the loyalty standard used for hiring or removing people in executive departments or agencies. It says employment can be refused or ended when there is a reasonable doubt about a person's loyalty to the Government of the United States. It affects people seeking or holding jobs in the executive branch.

10240.s: This order sets rules for ending the service of some women in the Regular Army, Navy, Marine Corps, and Air Force. It says their commission, warrant, or enlistment may be terminated for the same reasons and in the same way as male members of the same service and rank, or in certain cases involving children or pregnancy. It applies to women who are parents, have custody of a child, are step-parents with a child in the household for more than thirty days a year, are pregnant, or have given birth while serving.

10239.s: The order exempts Howell Cone, Collector of Customs for Customs Collection District No. 17 in Savannah, Georgia, from compulsory retirement for age. This exemption lasts for an indefinite period and cannot go beyond the appointment and qualification of his successor.

10238.s: This order makes changes in the customs field organization. It revokes the customs port of entry designations for Provincetown, Massachusetts, and Lewes, Delaware, extends the New London, Connecticut, port to include Groton, Connecticut, and designates Pelican, Alaska, as a customs port of entry.

10237.s: This order applies the provisions of the August 26, 1950 act to the Panama Canal and the Panama Railroad Company. It says this action is taken in the interests of national security. It also says the order does not change the authority given to the Secretary of the Army under another executive order.

10236.s: This order changes a previous order about the President's Commission on Migratory Labor. It says the commission will cease to exist at the end of May 31, 1951.

10235.s: The order approves a seal as the official seal of the Economic Stabilization Agency. The seal shows an American bald eagle on an oak branch in front of three spur gears, with the agency name around the edge.

10234.s: This order transfers jurisdiction over certain lands under the Bankhead-Jones Farm Tenant Act from the Department of Agriculture to the Department of the Interior. It says those lands will be administered and may be exchanged under the Taylor Grazing Act. It also withdraws certain public lands in Idaho from most public-land laws and reserves them for use by the Department of Agriculture.

10233.s: This order amends a prior order on wage stabilization and labor disputes. It reconstitutes the Wage Stabilization Board with 18 members from the public, labor, and business and industry, and lets the Board take up certain labor disputes that threaten work affecting national defense. The Board may make recommendations, and in some cases its decision can be binding if the parties agree. It also says wage actions must fit stabilization policies and not conflict with other listed labor laws.

10232.s:
This order amends Selective Service regulations. It changes the rules for certain male aliens who are not required to register, and it requires some of them to carry specific papers.
It also lets local boards issue permits for registrants to leave certain areas unless the trip is likely to interfere with their duties under the Selective Service Act. The order changes the time limits for appealing a local board classification based on where the registrant is located.

10231.s: This order extends Part I of Executive Order 10210 to the Tennessee Valley Authority. It lets the Board of Directors of the Tennessee Valley Authority carry out the functions and authority given in that part, subject to its limits and regulations. Any regulations the board writes do not need approval from the Secretary of Defense. It also says the order does not affect any other procurement authority the Tennessee Valley Authority or its board may already have.

10230.s: This order changes Selective Service rules for deferments based on work, study, and agriculture. It says some registrants may be considered necessary because of their jobs, research, medical work, or certain studies, and it lets the President set special categories and rules for deferment. It also says registrants in Class II-A because of study must be marked with “(S)” on their records.

10229.s: This order exempts Hugh H. Bennett, the Chief of the Soil Conservation Service, from compulsory retirement for age. The exemption lasts for one year, through April 30, 1952.

10228.s: This order designates the Inter-American Defense Board as a public international organization under the International Organizations Immunities Act. It gives the Board the privileges, exemptions, and immunities allowed by that law.

10227.s: This order extends part of Executive Order 10210 to the General Services Administration. It authorizes the Administrator of General Services to exercise the functions and authority given under that part for the agency, subject to its limits and regulations. The Administrator's regulations do not need approval by the Secretary of Defense, and the order does not affect any other procurement authority the agency or Administrator may already have.

10226.s: This order sets rules to safeguard vessels, harbors, ports, and waterfront facilities in the Canal Zone from sabotage, accidents, and other similar harm. It gives the Governor of The Panama Canal authority to enforce the rules, inspect and search vessels and waterfront facilities, control access, and require identification credentials. It also lets the Governor regulate dangerous cargo and requires sabotage or subversive activity to be reported right away. People who break the rules can face seizure of a vessel and criminal penalties.

10225.s: This order exempts Bernice Pyke, the Collector of Customs for Customs Collection District No. 41 in Cleveland, Ohio, from compulsory retirement for age. The exemption lasts for an indefinite period of time, but not beyond March 31, 1952, when her current term of office expires.

10224.s: This order creates the National Advisory Board on Mobilization Policy. The Board will advise the President on the current defense mobilization program, make recommendations and reports, and meet with the President when asked. Its members serve without pay, and some may be paid travel expenses and a per diem allowance while doing Board business.

10223.s: This order designates the Atomic Energy Commission as an additional guaranteeing agency under section 301 of the Defense Production Act of 1950. It also makes certain provisions of earlier executive orders apply to the Atomic Energy Commission the same way they apply to other guaranteeing agencies. It does not change Executive Order No. 10193.

10222.s: This order transfers certain civil defense health services and special weapons defense functions from the Health Resources Office of the National Security Resources Board to the Federal Civil Defense Administration. It also moves related property, records, and some personnel tied to those functions. The Federal Civil Defense Administrator keeps those functions under his jurisdiction until the President changes it.

10220.s: This order lets Stanley C. Wollaston be appointed to a competitive job in the Department of Labor without following the competitive rules of the Civil Service Act. It applies only to his appointment and waives those civil service requirements for that position.

10221.s: This order gives the Housing and Home Finance Administrator the President’s disaster relief duties under the act. The Administrator may direct federal agencies to help in a major disaster, coordinate their disaster assistance, and prepare proposed rules and reports for the President. Federal agencies may still give help under their own authority when disaster aid cannot wait for the President’s decision.

10219.s: This order gives federal officials duties for transportation and storage to support national defense and domestic and foreign commerce. It tells them to collect data, make plans, and coordinate the use of domestic transport, shipping, air transport, and other facilities. It also lets them allocate transportation and storage resources, set priorities, and work with other federal, state, and local agencies.

10218.s: This order reserves the airspace over the Las Vegas Project in Las Vegas, Nevada for national defense and other government purposes. No person may fly an aircraft in this area unless authorized by the United States Atomic Energy Commission. Anyone who flies there in violation of the order is subject to penalties under the Civil Aeronautics Act of 1938.

10217.s: This order changes a rule for certain federal employees who want to get competitive status. It says the head of their agency must recommend them to the Civil Service Commission within six months of the order. If an employee leaves a civilian job to enter the armed forces, the recommendation must be made within six months after the employee’s military service ends honorably.

10216.s: This order extends part of an earlier executive order to the Department of Agriculture, the Atomic Energy Commission, the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, and the Government Printing Office. It lets the heads of those agencies carry out the same functions and authority given to certain secretaries under that earlier order, subject to its limits and rules. It also says their own regulations do not need approval from the Secretary of Defense, and it does not take away any other procurement authority they may already have.

10215.s: This order exempts Arthur A. Quinn, the Comptroller of Customs with headquarters at New York, New York, from compulsory retirement for age. The exemption lasts for an indefinite period and cannot extend beyond June 30, 1951.

10214.s: This order sets the Manual for Courts-Martial, United States, 1951, for the armed forces. It applies to court-martial processes started on or after May 31, 1951, and it does not cancel investigations, trials, or other actions that began before that date. It also says the manual cannot make punishable any act done or omitted before its effective date if it was not punishable then, and it keeps the older maximum punishment for earlier offenses.

10213.s: This order includes certain lands in Cherokee County, North Carolina, and Polk County, Tennessee, as parts of the Nantahala National Forest and the Cherokee National Forest. It follows an agreement between the Tennessee Valley Authority and the Department of Agriculture that transfers rights in those lands to the department. The lands are to be reserved for national-forest purposes under the terms of that agreement.

10212.s: This order transfers the use, possession, and control of several lands and rights-of-way in the Cherokee National Forest in Polk County, Tennessee, from the Department of Agriculture to the Tennessee Valley Authority. It also gives the Tennessee Valley Authority rights of way for an access road and for telephone lines on certain strips of land. The order allows the removal of danger trees on adjoining land when needed to protect the telephone lines.

10211.s: This order puts section 31 of the Organic Act of Guam into operation as of January 1, 1951. It means the income-tax laws in force in the United States, and any future ones, are also in force in Guam.

10210.s: This order lets the Department of Defense enter into and change contracts for things and services needed for national defense, and it lets certain Defense officials delegate that authority. It also extends those same powers to the Department of Commerce, subject to the order’s limits and regulations. The order covers payments, claims, contract records, nondiscrimination, limits on fees and profits, and makes some labor laws still apply to covered contracts.

10209.s: This order amends rules for paying certain expenses connected with the death of some civilian officers and employees of the United States. It says allowed preparation costs include embalming, cremation, necessary clothing, and a casket. The total amount allowed for these preparation costs may not be more than $150.

10208.s: This order directs the Secretary of State to carry out the President’s powers under the Yugoslav Emergency Relief Assistance Act of 1950. It transfers $37,800,000 from the Economic Cooperation Administration to the Department of Agriculture. The money is to be administered under that relief law.

10206.s: This order lets the Secretary of State ask the Secretary of Defense to send armed forces personnel to the United Nations and provide facilities, services, supplies, and equipment. It applies only to United Nations activities aimed at the peaceful settlement of disputes and not those involving armed forces under Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter. It also requires reimbursement from the United Nations for these expenses, unless the Secretary of State waives all or part of it in exceptional circumstances or when it is in the national interest.

10205.s: This order changes earlier rules under the Defense Production Act of 1950 for appointing certain people in government departments and agencies. It lets department or agency heads hire persons of outstanding experience and ability without compensation, but they may not pass that authority to someone else. It also limits salary payments from sources other than the appointee’s private employer at the time of appointment and requires written certification for appointments to positions other than advisory or consultative.

10207.s: This order creates a commission in the Executive Office of the President called the President's Commission on Internal Security and Individual Rights. The commission is directed to study internal security and the protection of individual rights and freedoms, including laws and practices on treason, sabotage, espionage, and the Government employee loyalty and security programs. It must report its findings and recommendations to the President, and federal departments and agencies are directed to help it do its work.

10204.s: This order sets rules for paying basic allowances for quarters to members of the uniformed services. It says a member gets this allowance when entitled to receive basic pay, with rules for when quarters are considered assigned and when no allowance is paid. It also lets the Secretaries concerned issue extra rules for their services, and it becomes effective on February 1, 1951.

10202.s: This order changes Selective Service regulations on volunteers, local boards, and classification rules. It lets certain men volunteer for induction into the armed forces, sets how local boards handle volunteers, and allows panels of local boards when the workload is too great. It also changes some draft classification rules, including how certain registrants are placed in classes and when a Classification Questionnaire may be mailed to a registrant under 19 unless he first volunteers.

10203.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between American Airlines and certain employees represented by the Air Line Pilots Association, International. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the board reports, American Airlines and its employees may not change the conditions that led to the dispute unless they agree to do so.

10201.s: This order attaches the Virgin Islands to the internal revenue collection district of Maryland for all purposes allowed under the internal revenue laws of the United States. It takes effect on January 1, 1951.

10200.s: This order creates the Defense Production Administration and places it under a Defense Production Administrator appointed by the President with Senate consent. It gives the Administrator certain functions under the Defense Production Act, including priorities and allocations, requisitioning, voluntary agreements, and expanding production, capacity, and supply. It also says the Administrator and the Secretary of Agriculture will decide how to divide food supplies between industrial use and human and animal consumption when food is short. The order also creates the Defense Mobilization Board to advise the Director of Defense Mobilization.

10199.s: This order lets the Secretary of Agriculture issue regulations without the President’s approval when needed to carry out powers under the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act of 1937, as amended. It affects the Secretary of Agriculture and the people and businesses covered by those agricultural marketing rules.

10198.s: This order exempts Paul A. Walker from compulsory retirement for age. He may keep serving as a member of the Federal Communications Commission for an indefinite period, but not beyond the end of his current term.

10197.s: This order directs the Secretary of Commerce to use the powers given under section 102 of the Civil Aeronautics Act, as amended, while the order is in effect. It says the Secretary may use rules, regulations, or orders as needed to meet national security requirements for aircraft in flight.

10196.s: This order changes the rules for paying travel and transportation expenses for civilian officers and employees of the United States who are transferred for permanent duty. It covers travel for the employee and the immediate family, and it sets rules for shipment of household goods and personal effects. It also says some transfers and certain employees are not covered, and it adds limits and conditions for payment.

10195.s: This order designates Korea and the waters next to it as an area where U.S. armed forces have engaged in combat, for purposes of the Internal Revenue Code. It says the combatant activities in that area began on June 27, 1950.

10194.s: This order creates the Federal Safety Council in the Department of Labor. The council advises the Secretary of Labor on safety programs for civilian Federal employees and on ways to reduce work hazards, health risks, injuries, and accidents. It includes one representative from each executive department and agency and the Government of the District of Columbia. The order also revokes a prior safety council order and transfers its records to the new council.

10192.s: This order changes Executive Order No. 10129 by replacing one date with March 1, 1951. It also changes the words “Thirty days” to “Sixty days” in another paragraph. These changes affect the President’s Commission on Migratory Labor.

10193.s: This order creates the Office of Defense Mobilization in the Executive Office of the President and sets up a Director to lead it, appointed by the President with Senate consent. The Director is given control and coordination over Executive Branch mobilization work, including production, procurement, manpower, stabilization, and transport. Federal agencies and departments must follow the Director’s directives and provide reports when required.

10190.s: This order sets rules for asking for a new trial or other relief in Navy and Coast Guard court-martial cases involving offenses committed during World War II. An accused, or a representative, may file one written petition asking for a new trial, for a sentence to be vacated, or for rights, privileges, or property to be restored. Relief may be granted only if the reviewing official finds good cause and decides that an injustice resulted from the findings or sentence. If a new trial is granted, the person is brought before a new court on the same charges, unless the problem was with the charges themselves.

10191.s: This order extends the period of trust or other restrictions against alienation in patents for Indian lands that would otherwise expire during the calendar year 1951. The extension is for 25 more years from the date the trust would otherwise end. It applies to tribal and individual Indian lands, except in cases where Congress has specifically kept the power to extend the trust period for itself.

10188.s: This order designates and authorizes Honorable Luis Negron-Fernandez to serve as Acting Judge for the United States District Court for the District of Puerto Rico. He may perform the judge’s duties and sign needed papers and records when the judge is absent, ill, or otherwise legally unable to serve during 1951, without extra pay.

10189.s: This order changes the rules for awarding the Distinguished Flying Cross. It sets time limits for when the medal can be awarded for acts of heroism or extraordinary achievement, including special rules for acts during World War II and the period after September 2, 1945. It also says that if a recommendation was lost, certain officer certificates or enlisted affidavits may be accepted so the case can be reviewed on its merits.

10187.s: This order amends an earlier executive order about allowances and allotments for Government personnel on foreign duty. It gives the Secretary of State authority over regulations for civilian officers and employees on living-quarters allowances, cost-of-living allowances, and representation allowances.

10186.s: This order establishes the Federal Civil Defense Administration in the Executive Office of the President to promote and help coordinate civil defense in the United States with the States. It directs the Administration to prepare civil defense plans, support research and training, share information, help arrange mutual aid agreements, and make provision for civil defense communications. Federal departments and agencies must cooperate with the Administrator, and some civil defense work from the National Security Resources Board is transferred to the new Administration.

10185.s: This order changes the name of the National Advisory Committee from “Doctors, Dentists, and Allied Specialists” to “Physicians, Dentists, and Allied Specialists.” It also says the Selective Service System shall pay necessary expenses of the Committee, including member compensation, and the necessary expenses of any state and local volunteer advisory committees the Committee designates, within the limits of applicable law.

10184.s: This order transfers a portion of the Arecibo Coast Guard Lighthouse Reservation at Arecibo Harbor, Puerto Rico, to the Insular Government of Puerto Rico. The land had been reserved for lighthouse purposes, but the order says it is no longer needed for those or other United States purposes. It also modifies the 1903 proclamation that reserved the land.

10182.s: This order lets department and agency heads hire people with outstanding experience and ability without pay, and also hire experts, consultants, and outside agencies or volunteers under the Defense Production Act. It says these appointments should mostly be advisory or consultative, and the government should try to avoid conflicts between official duties and private interests. People hired under the order are exempt from certain conflict of interest laws, but the order keeps some limits on contracts, claims against the Government, and some salary arrangements.

10183.s: This order changes internal revenue collection district boundaries in New York. It moves the Country of Richmond (Staten Island) from the first district to the second district, and it also moves a described area from the third district to the second district.

10181.s: This order gives the Director of the Bureau of the Budget the job of deciding which agency programs are directly related to the national defense under a specific law. It affects agency programs that are considered directly tied to national defense.

10180.s: This order says that, for a period tied to the interest of the national defense, most new appointments in the executive branch must be nonpermanent, with some exceptions for Presidential appointees, postmasters, and certain cases approved by the Civil Service Commission or agency heads. It also says many promotions, transfers between agencies, and some reemployment of former Federal employees must be nonpermanent, and it sets rules for reemployment rights. People given nonpermanent appointments under the order are excluded from the Civil Service Retirement Act unless they are eligible through continuity of service, reinstatement, or another basis.

10179.s: This order establishes the Korean Service Medal for members of the U.S. armed forces who served in the area or areas of military operations in the Korean theater during the covered period. The Secretaries of the Army, Navy, and Air Force are to issue uniform regulations for the award, with approval from the Secretary of Defense. No one may receive more than one medal, and it may be awarded after death.

10178.s: This order reserves certain real and personal property in Guam for the United States and places some of it under the control of the Secretary of the Navy. It says some of that property must be transferred to the Department of the Army, the Department of the Air Force, and the Coast Guard if needed for their purposes. It also keeps certain lands under the administrative supervision of the Secretary of the Interior for possible disposition, and leaves other personal property with the federal department or agency that already has it.

10176.s: This order suspends compliance with certain employment rules in the Canal Zone under the General Appropriation Act, 1951. It does not change the provisions about how much compensation may be received by people in skilled, technical, clerical, administrative, executive, or supervisory jobs there when they are employed by the United States Government or by a company partly or wholly owned by it.

10175.s: This order changes two earlier orders about land handled under the Bankhead-Jones Farm Tenant Act. It replaces one agency name with the Bureau of Land Management and adds that lands exchanged for reserved public lands are still covered by that act’s rules. It also transfers jurisdiction over certain lands, waters, water rights, improvements, and structures to the Department of the Interior, including lands being acquired once that acquisition is complete.

10177.s: This order changes the rules for travel and transportation expenses for some new government appointees outside the United States. New appointees must agree in writing to stay in government service, and if they break that agreement, the United States can recover the money it spent. Return travel expenses after separation are allowed only after at least one year of service, or up to three years if set in advance by the department or agency head, unless the separation is for reasons beyond the person's control.

10174.s: This order changes a prior order that set regulations under the Career Compensation Act of 1949. It says those regulations will stay in effect until January 31, 1951, to the extent they are required or allowed under section 302 of that law. It takes effect on November 1, 1950.

10172.s: This order designates the Chairman of the National Security Resources Board as the certifying authority under section 124A of the Internal Revenue Code. The Chairman is to use government departments and agencies to handle applications for necessity certificates about the amortization of emergency facilities. The order also says the Chairman should work with industries and develop programs for expanding capacity.

10173.s: This order sets rules to protect vessels, harbors, ports, and waterfront facilities in the United States from sabotage, subversive acts, accidents, and similar harm. It gives the Coast Guard power to enforce the rules, inspect and search vessels and waterfront facilities, control access, and supervise or control vessel movement when needed. It also lets officials require identification for access, regulate dangerous cargo, and require reports of sabotage or subversive activity. Violations can lead to seizure of a vessel and criminal penalties.

10170.s: This order amends a prior executive order that set up the Interdepartmental Committee on Trade Agreements and the Committee for Reciprocity Information. It adds the Secretary of the Interior to the list of agency heads whose departments are represented on those committees. This affects the committees involved in administering reciprocal trade-agreements programs.

10169.s: This order creates the National Advisory Committee on Mobilization Policy to advise the National Security Resources Board on national mobilization policy. The committee’s members are to be appointed by the Board’s Chairman and are to represent business, labor, agriculture, and the public as a whole. Federal departments and agencies are asked to help the committee and provide information it needs. The National Security Resources Board is to pay the committee’s necessary expenses within the limits of applicable law.

10168.s: This order sets rules for extra pay for enlisted members of the uniformed services for sea duty and foreign duty. It says who counts as being on sea duty or foreign duty, and it excludes some kinds of duty from those pay rules. A member cannot receive both kinds of pay for the same period. It also lets the service secretaries issue more rules to carry it out.

10167.s: This order sets rules for the registration, classification, physical examination, selection, and induction of male persons in medical, dental, and allied specialist categories under the Selective Service Act. It requires these men to register during a special registration period and follow the forms and procedures set by the Selective Service System. It also tells local boards how to handle records and how to classify special registrants, including when they may be placed in deferment or exempt classes.

10166.s: This order establishes a National Advisory Committee on the Selection of Doctors, Dentists, and Allied Specialists. The committee is to advise the Selective Service System and coordinate with state and local volunteer advisory committees on choosing needed medical, dental, and allied specialist personnel. It also says the committee should consult with certain federal officials and agencies, and federal departments and agencies are asked to cooperate and provide information.

10163.s:
This order creates the Armed Forces Reserve Medal for members and former members of the reserve components of the armed forces, including the Coast Guard Reserve and the Marine Corps Reserve. It sets rules for the medal’s design and for who may receive it.

The medal may be awarded to people who complete ten years of honorable service in one or more reserve components within twelve consecutive years. It also says the medal may be given instead of the Naval Reserve or Marine Corps Reserve Medal in some cases, and only one medal may be awarded to any one person.

10164.s: This order extends for twelve months all enlistments in the United States Coast Guard, including the Coast Guard Reserve, that would expire after the date of the order and before July 9, 1951. It does not stop voluntary re-enlistment or voluntary extension of existing enlistments under applicable laws or Coast Guard regulations, and it directs the Secretary of the Treasury to take the steps needed to carry it out.

10162.s: This order authorizes the appointment of Frederick C. Kilguss as Deputy Administrative Assistant Attorney General in the Department of Justice. It allows that appointment to be made without following the competitive provisions of the Civil Service Rules and Regulations.

10161.s: This order gives parts of the President’s powers under the Defense Production Act of 1950 to several federal officials and agencies. It assigns duties for priorities and allocations of materials, transportation, production, financing, price and wage stabilization, real estate credit, labor supply, and voluntary agreements. It affects federal departments and agencies that deal with energy, food, transportation, defense production, labor, housing, and credit.

10160.s: This order requires people who sold or delivered goods or services, or offered them for sale or delivery, between May 24, 1950, and June 24, 1950, to keep records about the prices they received or asked and the costs they incurred. It does not apply to an individual's wage or salary records, sales of agricultural commodities by the producer, or certain records and rates listed in the order. The order defines terms like "person," "prices," and "goods" for these record-keeping rules.

10158.s: This order further amends an earlier order that set regulations for certain parts of the Career Compensation Act of 1949. It keeps those regulations in effect until October 31, 1950, for the provisions covered by sections 206 and 302 of that law.

10159.s: The order gives the Secretary of State the authority to carry out most of the powers under the Act for International Development and to plan and run the programs it authorizes. It also directs other departments and agencies to take part when asked, as long as it is allowed by law. The order creates an International Development Advisory Board to advise on general policy matters and tells the Secretary of State to set up an Interdepartmental Advisory Council on Technical Cooperation.

10156.s: This order sets who will act as Secretary of the Interior if the Secretary is dead, resigns, is absent, or is sick. It says the Under Secretary will serve first, then the ranking Assistant Secretary, and then the Solicitor if needed. It also says how to decide which Assistant Secretary ranks first and replaces an earlier order on this same subject.

10157.s: This order lets some Federal Government employees without competitive status gain competitive status if they meet the listed service, rating, recommendation, and examination requirements. It applies to employees in the competitive service who are in active-duty status, including those on active military duty, and it says military service does not count as a break in service. It does not apply to postmasters, some rural carriers, or people in positions limited by law or executive order to preference eligibles. The Civil Service Commission is told to issue rules to carry out the order.

10155.s: This order takes possession, control, and operation of the transportation systems of the listed railroads through the Secretary of the Army. It says this is because labor disturbances are causing interruptions or threatened interruptions in railroad service. The order is meant to keep transportation service continuous and uninterrupted, and it affects the railroads named in the attached list.

10154.s: This order sets a line of succession for the Postmaster General. If both the Postmaster General and the Deputy Postmaster General die, resign, are absent, or are sick, the highest listed Assistant Postmaster General who is able to serve would perform the duties of that office. The order applies to certain officers in the Post Office Department.

10152.s: This order sets regulations for incentive pay for members of the uniformed services who perform hazardous duty under competent orders. It defines several kinds of duty, including aerial flight, submarine duty, glider flights, parachute jumping, leprosy duty, demolition of explosives, and certain diving and training duties. It also sets minimum flight, jump, and other requirements that members must meet to qualify for the pay.

10153.s: This order sets rules for counting travel time as active duty for members of the uniformed services called or ordered to active duty for more than thirty days. If public transportation is used, the travel time is based on actual schedules; if private conveyance is specifically authorized, travel time is figured by miles traveled. It also says private conveyance may not be specifically authorized for calls to active duty of less than ninety consecutive days, and it allows the Secretaries concerned to issue supplementary regulations.

10149.s: This order suspends some limits on punishments for future violations of certain Articles of War. It applies to persons under the command of, or within any area controlled by, the Commander in Chief, Far East, or any successor in command. The articles cover desertion, helping or advising desertion, absence without leave, assaulting or willfully disobeying a superior officer, insubordinate conduct toward a noncommissioned officer, and misbehavior of sentinels.

10150.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate disputes between the Atlantic & East Carolina Railway Company, other listed carriers, and certain employees represented by listed labor organizations. The board must report its findings to the President, and the carriers and employees may not change the conditions behind the disputes except by agreement while the order is in effect and after the board reports for the period set by the Railway Labor Act.

10148.s: This order names Commerce Department officers who may perform the duties of the Secretary of Commerce if the Secretary is absent, sick, resigns, or dies. It gives that role first to the Under Secretary of Commerce for Transportation, then to the Assistant Secretaries of Commerce in order of precedence, and then to the Solicitor of Commerce. It also replaces an earlier order on the same subject.

10146.s: This order exempts William J. Patterson, a member of the Interstate Commerce Commission, from compulsory retirement for age. The exemption lasts for an indefinite period, but not beyond the end of his current term of office. For this order, his term ends when a successor is appointed and qualified.

10147.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the New York Central Railroad Company, Lines East of Buffalo, and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. For that period, and for thirty days after the report, the company and its employees may not change the conditions that caused the dispute except by agreement.

10145.s: This order extends enlistments in the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Naval Reserve, Marine Corps Reserve, and any part of the Air Force that would expire after July 27, 1950, and before July 9, 1951. It also says this does not stop voluntary re-enlistments or voluntary extensions under the laws and rules that apply. The Secretary of Defense is directed to take any steps needed to carry out the order.

10144.s: This order amends an earlier order about the United States High Commissioner for Germany. It gives the High Commissioner responsibility for the custody, care, and sentence execution of war criminals confined in Germany, including decisions on pardon, clemency, parole, or release in certain cases. It also changes one job title in the earlier order to "Commander in Chief, European Command."

10143.s: This order allows Mrs. Ruth Edna McC. Somers to be appointed to an appropriate position in the competitive service of the Government without regard to the Civil Service Rules. It says she is the widow of Andrew Lawrence Somers, who served for more than twenty-four years in the House of Representatives from New York.

10142.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate a dispute between Braniff Airways and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, Braniff Airways and its employees may not change the conditions that led to the dispute except by agreement.

10141.s: This order takes possession and control of the Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Railroad Company’s transportation system because of a labor disturbance and directs the Secretary of the Army to operate it. It says the system should keep providing continuous transportation service, and company management, board members, officers, and employees may continue their usual work unless the Secretary orders otherwise. Existing contracts stay in effect, and workers keep the right to join labor organizations and bargain collectively unless those activities interfere with operating the system.

10139.s: The order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Toledo Lakefront Dock Company and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, the company and its employees cannot change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

10140.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Pullman Company and certain employees represented by the Order of Railway Conductors. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. From this order’s date and for thirty days after the report is made, the Pullman Company and its employees may not change the conditions that led to the dispute except by agreement.

10138.s: The order creates a three-member board to investigate a labor dispute between the Toledo, Lorain & Fairport Dock Company and certain of its employees represented by the International Longshoremen's Association. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the company and its employees may not change the conditions that led to the dispute unless they agree.

10137.s: This order changes the effective date of an earlier order that transfers the administration of Guam from the Secretary of the Navy to the Secretary of the Interior. It also changes the effective date of the revocation of Executive Order No. 108-A to August 1, 1950.

10136.s: This order changes Executive Order 10084, which set regulations under the Career Compensation Act of 1949. It keeps some of those regulations in effect until August 31, 1950, and others until September 30, 1950.

10135.s: This order extends the suspension of the eight-hour law for laborers and mechanics employed by the Department of the Army or the Department of the Air Force on certain public works. It applies when the Secretary of the Army or the Secretary of the Air Force finds the suspension essential for military or naval supply and maintenance, essential construction, or international commitments. The order also says these workers must be paid on a basic eight-hour day rate, with overtime paid at time and one-half for hours over eight in a day. It becomes effective on July 1, 1950, and extends the suspension to July 1, 1951.

10133.s: This order designates the Organization for European Economic Cooperation as a public international organization. It gives that organization the privileges, exemptions, and immunities under the International Organizations Immunities Act.

10134.s: This order extends the existence of the Quetico-Superior Committee for four more years. It keeps the committee in place from June 30, 1950, to June 30, 1954.

10132.s: This order allows the Senate Special Committee to inspect certain tax returns for periods through 1949. The returns covered include income, excess profits, declared value excess-profits, capital stock, estate, and gift tax returns. The inspection is for carrying out the Senate resolution and is subject to the stated Treasury conditions.

10130.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Boston & Albany Railroad Company and certain of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. For that period, and for thirty days after the report, the company and its employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

10128.s: This order changes the membership of the National Capital Housing Authority. It says the authority shall include certain officials of the United States and the District of Columbia government, plus three other officials chosen by the President of the United States.

10129.s: This order creates the President's Commission on Migratory Labor, made up of a chairman and four other members chosen by the President. The commission is directed to study the conditions of migratory workers, the problems caused by worker migration into the United States, agricultural labor needs, and the extent of illegal migration of foreign workers. It must report its findings and recommendations to the President, and federal agencies are directed to help it with information and assistance.

10126.s: This order reserves the airspace over certain parts of Washington, D.C. for national defense, other government purposes, and public safety. No one may fly an aircraft in that airspace unless the Administrator of Civil Aeronautics gives special permission. People who violate the order can be subject to penalties under the Civil Aeronautics Act of 1938.

10127.s: This order reserves the airspace over three United States Atomic Energy Commission facilities for national defense and other government purposes. The areas are the Clinton Engineering Works in Oak Ridge, Tennessee; the Hanford Engineer Works in Richland, Washington; and the Los Alamos Project in Santa Fe, New Mexico. No one may navigate an aircraft in these airspace reservations except by authority of the United States Atomic Energy Commission. People who violate the order are subject to the penalties in the Civil Aeronautics Act of 1938.

10125.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Chicago & Illinois Midland Railway Company and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that period, and for thirty days after the report, neither side may change the working conditions tied to the dispute unless both agree.

10124.s: This order sets rules for certain members and former members of the uniformed services to choose between disability retirement pay, disability severance pay, or retired pay under the Career Compensation Act of 1949. The Secretary concerned must tell each affected person about the benefits they may get, their right to make an election, and the effect of the law on disability retirement pay. They will keep getting retired pay under the old rules unless they choose a different method of payment before October 1, 1954, and qualify for it.

10122.s: This order sets rules for paying disability retirement pay, and for hospitalization and re-examination, for members and former members of the uniformed services. It shifts many of those duties to the Secretary concerned, and in some cases to the Secretary of the Army, Secretary of the Air Force, or the Administrator of Veterans' Affairs. It also keeps some Public Health Service duties in place and makes special rules for hospitalization for chronic diseases.

10123.s: This order revokes two earlier executive orders about the organization of the Navy Department and the Naval Establishment. It also says this revocation does not bring back two other executive orders that had been revoked by the earlier order.

10121.s: This order transfers title to a tract of public land next to Honolulu Airport to the Territory of Hawaii. The land is described as part of the airport extension and is needed for the airport's operation. The order also lets the United States Department of Defense keep using Areas 3 and 4 for certain military uses, and it reserves the right to use the East-West runway and related taxi strips for flights into and out of Hickam Air Force Base.

10119.s: This order sets rules for paying basic allowances for subsistence to members of the uniformed services. It says enlisted members who are fed by the government but are away from their station during a meal get one-third of the daily allowance for that meal. It also lets certain agency heads issue supplemental regulations for their personnel, and it keeps existing subsistence rules in effect until May 1, 1950.

10120.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between certain carriers and some of their employees represented by the Railroad Yardmasters of America. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. For that period, and for thirty days after the report, the carriers and their employees may not change the conditions that gave rise to the dispute except by agreement.

10117.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the carriers represented by the Western Carriers' Conference Committee and certain of their employees represented by the Switchmen's Union of North America. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the carriers and their employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute unless they agree to do so.

10118.s: This order changes the ending date for part of Executive Order 10084, which set regulations under the Career Compensation Act of 1949. It says the order was in effect from October 1, 1949, and would stop on March 31, 1950, except for the regulations under certain sections of the act. Those specific regulations would stay in effect until June 30, 1950.

10116.s: This order amends the Selective Service Regulations and updates the National Selective Service Appeal Board. It says the board is a civilian appeal agency within the Selective Service System, with three presidential appointees, and it can perform certain functions given to the President on appeals about training and service. It also changes rules on registrant classifications, delinquent registrants, appeal records, and transfers for armed forces physical examinations.

10115.s: This order restores a tract of land near Puolo Point on the Island of Kauai to the jurisdiction of the Territory of Hawaii. The land had been reserved for military purposes, but the order says it is no longer needed for that use.

10114.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Terminal Railroad Association of St. Louis and certain of its employees. The dispute involves employees represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen and Enginemen. The board must report its findings to the President, and no changes may be made by the railroad or its employees in the conditions involved except by agreement until the board reports.

10113.s: This order gives the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of the Treasury authority to set the amount and kind of clothing furnished to enlisted people in the armed forces, and to set cash allowances when clothing is not furnished. It applies to enlisted persons of either sex in the listed services. Existing rules stay in place until changed, revoked, or replaced under this order.

10112.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between certain railroad carriers and some of their employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. For thirty days after the report, the carriers and employees named in the order cannot change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

10111.s: This order approves a seal as the official seal of the Central Intelligence Agency. The seal includes a compass rose, an American bald eagle's head, and the words “United States of America” and “Central Intelligence Agency.” It applies to the Central Intelligence Agency.

10110.s: This order creates the President's Communications Policy Board, made up of a chairman and four other members chosen by the President. The board is to study how radio and wire communications are used by government and non-government groups and make recommendations to the President on communications policy.
