It also sets rules for noncommissioned officers, previous convictions, and when sentences may be reduced or suspended.

3363.s: The order extends the trust period on the allotments of the Ponca Indians in Oklahoma for another 25 years. It applies to the Ponca Indians in Oklahoma and follows an earlier one-year extension.

3365.s: This order extends the trust or other period of restriction against alienation in certain patents already issued to Indians for lands on the public domain. It applies for a further period of twenty-five years from the date the trust would otherwise expire.

3360.s: This order directs that an official flag be made for the Secretary of State. The flag is to be dark blue with the Department of State arms in white in the center and a gold star on each side. It also directs that the flag be displayed on the vessel carrying the Secretary of State on a ceremonial visit to certain States of South America, and on the launch used to take him to shore when needed.

3336.s: The order directs the United States flag to be shown at half-mast on Sunday, November 14, 1920. It applies at military posts, naval stations, on vessels, and on U.S. buildings as part of memorial services for Americans who died in the World War.

3338.s: This order changes the rules for filling vacancies in postmaster jobs at first, second, and third class post offices. If a vacancy is not filled by a qualified person in the competitive classified civil service, the Civil Service Commission must hold an open competitive examination and certify the result to the Postmaster General. A person who has passed his sixty-fifth birthday or who has not lived within the delivery of the office for the two years before the vacancy cannot take the examination.

3332.s: The order directs the War Department to keep control of certain Hoboken piers, bulkhead space, office space, and yard space. It covers piers 1, 4, 5, 6, and 11, along with nearby areas named in the order. Pier 1 is to be kept for the length of an existing five-year lease, and the other property for two years unless the President later says the need has ended.

3313.s: The order changes rules on seamen’s wages for vessels of the United States. It says seamen can demand part of wages owed at certain ports and must get the rest when the voyage ends. It also makes it unlawful to pay wages before they are earned or to take pay for helping a seaman get employment, and this applies to seamen shipped in foreign ports too.

3320.s: This order directs the United States Grain Corporation to wind up and liquidate its remaining business, property, and affairs. It also ends the United States Food Administration and transfers certain records, accounts, and property to the Treasury Department or the Grain Corporation. Any remaining assets of the Grain Corporation are to be paid into the Treasury of the United States.

3294.s: The order changes rules for people defined as hostile or enemy aliens who want to leave a U.S. port. They generally do not need a U.S. permit to depart unless the Secretary of State orders otherwise, but they must show a passport from their own government and a certificate showing compliance with the income tax law. It also says no passport or permit is required for travel between the continental United States and Newfoundland or the St. Pierre and Miquelon Islands, except for travel through those places en route to or from the United States.

3235.s: This order directs the Director General of Railroads and his representatives to keep the powers they were given over coal delivery, use, consumption, distribution, and apportionment after March 1, 1920. It affects the Director General of Railroads and the people and businesses involved in coal distribution. It also keeps in place the authority described in two earlier orders from 1919.

3292.s: The order directs the United States Grain Corporation to reduce its outstanding capital stock from Five Hundred Million Dollars to One Hundred and Fifty Million Dollars. It also directs Julius H. Barnes to arrange the reduction, surrender Three Million Five Hundred Thousand shares for cancellation, and pay Three Hundred and Fifty Million Dollars into the Treasury of the United States as miscellaneous receipts.

3231.s: This order changes the rules for certain people who may be defined as alien enemies. It says they do not need a U.S. permit before leaving by ship from a U.S. port for a European port, if they show a passport issued, renewed, or visaed by their own government within the last six months and a certificate showing compliance with the income tax law.

3206.s: This order creates a Board of Surveys and Maps to coordinate map-making and surveying work across government departments. The board is made up of one representative from each listed agency, and they serve without extra pay. It must make recommendations, settle certain disputes about surveys and maps, hold meetings, and set up a central information office in the U.S. Geological Survey to collect and share map and survey data.

3182.s: This order changes the pay and travel rules for people hired in the United States for the permanent force of the Panama Canal. Their pay starts when they leave the United States by ship, and they get free transportation and meals on the steamer, but not pay or travel expenses to the port. Former employees with less than one year of prior service are paid only from the date they enter service on the Isthmus, and hourly workers are paid for transit time on an eight-hour day basis. Salary for the trip to the Isthmus is not paid unless service there continues for thirty days, except in cases of discharge or other separation beyond the employee's control.

3204.s: This order extends the trust or other restriction on selling certain land patents issued to any Indian for lands on the public domain. It applies in cases where that restriction would otherwise expire during the calendar year nineteen hundred and twenty.

3176.s: The order takes possession and title of certain vessels for the United States under a 1917 joint resolution. It covers vessels within U.S. jurisdiction that were owned in whole or in part by German corporations, citizens, or subjects, or that flew the German flag or were under German register. The order says these vessels had been taken over during the war and are now taken over in accordance with the joint resolution.

3024.s: This order extends for one year the trust or other restriction on selling land in patents issued to Indians for lands on the public domain if that restriction would otherwise end during 1919. It does not apply to the specific cases listed in the order. It affects Indian patentees whose restriction periods were set to expire in that year.

2868.s: This order establishes the War Industries Board as a separate administrative agency to act for the President and under his direction. It keeps in effect the Board’s functions, duties, and powers as set out in a March 4, 1918 letter to its chairman.

2859.s: This order sets out the work of the National Research Council. It says the Council should stimulate research in the sciences, help use scientific resources for research projects, and promote cooperation among researchers at home and abroad. It also says the Government will be represented on the Council by officers or employees from specified executive branch departments and agencies.

2789.s: This order reserves about 94,000 acres in Arizona from all forms of disposal. It sets the land aside temporarily for Navajo Indians living there until allotments can be made in severalty or other provision can be made for their welfare. The withdrawal is subject to prior valid rights and claims, and it replaces an earlier order with the same purpose.

2796.s: This order sets rules for foreign exchange, exports of gold, silver, coin, bullion, and currency, and transfers of credit, securities, and property between the United States and foreign countries. It requires dealers to get registration certificates, file reports, keep records, and let their books be inspected. It also lets the Federal Reserve Board restrict or stop transactions with foreign correspondents and requires declarations that they will not deal with enemies or allies of enemies of the United States.

2777.s: This order sets rules for changing local laws in the Virgin Islands. Changes by the Colonial Council take effect only when approved by the Governor, and the President may disapprove them. It also says duties and taxes collected there, minus collection costs, must be used for the government and benefit of the islands. The Governor may authorize extra spending for expenses that were formerly paid by Denmark and for other necessary, unforeseen government expenses.

2778.s: This order extends for one year the trust or other restriction against selling land in patents issued to any Indian for lands on the public domain. It applies to cases where that restriction would otherwise expire during the calendar year nineteen hundred and eighteen, except for the specific named patentees listed in the order.

2774-A.s: The order creates a Division of Foreign Picture Service under the Committee on Public Information. It is meant to stimulate interest in the war and give entertainment and instruction through motion pictures to American soldiers at home and abroad. It also says the division will help the armies and citizens of U.S. allies through the Young Men's Christian Association and similar agencies.

2770.s: This order bars foreign insurance companies from doing business in the United States after February 1, 1918, unless they first get a license from the Secretary of the Treasury. It gives the Secretary of the Treasury power to issue or refuse those licenses. It affects foreign insurance companies that want to do business through agencies, branch offices, or other means in the United States.

2748.s: This order takes over the steam tug Pollux for the United States. It says the vessel had been owned in whole or in part by Germany or was flying the German flag or under German register. The United States Shipping Board may repair, equip, and man the vessel, and may operate, lease, or charter it in United States service or in other commerce.

2765.s: This order directs the United States Food Administrator to make and enforce rules for licensees under section 5 of the Food Control Act. It says he may act when a storage charge, commission, profit, or practice is unjust, unreasonable, discriminatory, unfair, or wasteful. It also says a just and fair profit is the normal average profit from the same business before July 1, 1914, under free competitive conditions, and he may set a margin over cost to match that profit and stop higher profits.

2741.s: This order lets the Postmaster General appoint newspaper readers and translators to certain confidential jobs under the Trading with the Enemy Act without a civil service examination during the war with Germany. It applies to those selected for these positions in the Post Office Department. The Civil Service Commission agrees because the jobs are highly confidential and require special qualifications.

2744.s: This order fixes the Alien Property Custodian’s salary at $5,000 a year and requires a $100,000 bond approved by the Attorney General. It gives the custodian power to hire staff, set their pay, and handle money and property in the United States that belong to enemies or allies of enemies under the Trading with the Enemy Act. It also lets the custodian designate banks or trust companies as depositaries and sets aside funds for the Alien Property Custodian, the Federal Trade Commission, the Secretary of the Treasury, and the War Trade Board.

2734.s: This order lets civilian employees of the Commissions on Training Camp Activities be appointed without following Civil Service rules. It also moves staffs that had been paid from private funds into the War and Navy Departments, with pay coming from government appropriations. The order says the established organizations should be continued.

2736.s: This order directs Herbert Hoover, as United States Food Administrator, to requisition any foods and feeds and storage facilities for them that he deems needed for public use connected with the common defense. It does not apply to support of the Army or the maintenance of the Navy. It also requires that just compensation be determined and paid.

2730.s: This order says American consular officers must provide certain listed services free of charge during the war and until further orders. It applies to any person in the military or naval service of the United States.

2729-A.s: This order sets up several boards and officials to carry out powers under the Trading with the Enemy Act and the espionage act. It gives them control over licenses for exports, imports, trade with enemies and enemy allies, foreign exchange, communications, censorship, patents, and foreign-language publications. It also transfers duties from the Exports Administrative Board, creates an Alien Property Custodian role, and gives that custodian power over property owed to or held for enemies and enemy allies.

2720.s: This order directs the Chief of Staff of the United States Army to do the duties of Secretary of War when the Secretary of War is ill or temporarily away from the seat of Government. It applies only when the Assistant Secretary of War is also absent.

2718.s: This order suspends the law that limited workers to eight hours of labor in one day on the construction of the new Immigration Station in Baltimore, Maryland. It says the work is being done for the early completion of buildings for military purposes during a national emergency. It also says workers on the job must be paid at a basic eight-hour day rate, with overtime paid at not less than time and one-half for hours over eight.

2709.s: The order takes immediate possession and title of the German motor vessel Hermes, which is at Honolulu, for the United States. It also orders the Secretary of the Navy to operate and equip the vessel in the service of the Navy until further directions.

2708.s: This order creates three new divisions under the Committee on Public Information: a Division of Pictures, a Division of Films, and a Division of Publications. It says their purpose is to stimulate recruiting and patriotic interest in the war and to seek cooperation from citizens for the war effort. It also authorizes the Secretary of State, the Secretary of War, and the Secretary of the Navy to detail officers to work with the committee.

2717.s: This order makes certain quarantine laws and rules apply in St. Thomas, St. Croix, and St. John in the West Indies Islands. It also takes public property of the former Virgin Islands government for United States use for quarantine purposes. The Secretary of the Treasury is given charge of the quarantine service, through the Surgeon General of the Public Health Service.

2697.s: This order puts the Secretary of the Treasury in charge of rules for exporting coin, bullion, and currency. Anyone who wants to export these items from the United States or its territorial possessions to certain foreign countries must file a sworn application with the local Federal reserve bank. The Federal reserve bank forwards the application and its recommendation to the Federal Reserve Board, which may allow or refuse the exportation with approval from the Secretary of the Treasury.

2705.s: The order suspends the eight-hour daily work limit for mechanics and laborers on certain Bureau of Standards contracts. It applies to work on an emergency laboratory building and other buildings used for research, testing, and experimental work during the present national emergency. It affects people working under those contracts for the Department of Commerce.

2696.s: This order suspends the law that required United States officers to survey, inspect, and measure foreign-built ships admitted to United States registry. The suspension applies to those ships for two years from September 1, 1917, if the Secretary of Commerce is satisfied that a ship is safe and seaworthy and that proper effort is being made to comply with the law. It affects foreign-built ships admitted to United States registry under the law.

2694-A.s: This order puts the Treasury Department in charge of carrying out sections 15 and 16 of the Food Control Act as they relate to distilled spirits. It gives the Secretary of the Treasury authority to assign duties to the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, Internal Revenue officers, the Division of Customs, and other assistants as needed. It also modifies an earlier executive order on the United States Food Administration where it conflicts with this order.

2692.s: This order establishes defensive sea areas at the terminal ports of the Panama Canal and sets their outer and inner limits. It requires vessels to use designated entrances, wait for permission from the Harbor Entrance Patrol, and follow its instructions before crossing the areas. It also limits vessel speed, restricts night crossings and bad-weather crossings, and allows vessels or people who break the rules to be detained.

2691.s: This order sets rules for how local laws in the Virgin Islands can be repealed, changed, or amended. It says those changes take effect when approved by the governor, and the President may disapprove and set aside any action by the Colonial Council. It also says duties and taxes collected in the Virgin Islands must be spent for the government and benefit of the islands under the local budget rules, with extra spending allowed for certain current expenses.

2690.s: This order appoints Harry A. Garfield as United States Fuel Administrator. He is to oversee and carry out the parts of the act that apply to fuel, including issuing, regulating, and revoking licenses. He may hire assistants, subordinates, and counsel and set their pay. Government departments and agencies are directed to cooperate with him.

2687.s: This order gives the Secretary of the Navy the President’s power under two laws tied to naval emergency and emergency shipping funds. It lets the Secretary use that power for building Navy vessels, making contracts for them, and getting materials, war materials, equipment, and munitions for the Navy. The Secretary may use these powers himself or through other officers who can make contracts for the government.

2681.s: This order creates a Delaware corporation called the Food Administration Grain Corporation. The United States Food Administrator is directed to form it, and the United States is to buy and own its stock except for small qualifying shares for directors or incorporators. The corporation is set up to buy, store, and sell wheat, flour, meal, beans, and potatoes at reasonable prices. Its board has seven members, and its officers must be chosen with the President’s approval.

2673-A.s: The order directs federal officials to use great care when issuing affidavits that could excuse drafted men from military service. It covers certain United States employees, including people who work with the mails and workers in armories, arsenals, and navy yards, if they are needed and cannot be replaced without substantial loss of efficiency. It also sets out a process for department officials to approve or disapprove exemption requests and says the same general method should be used for some other federal agencies when practical.

2670.s: This order takes over the former Virgin Islands government property used for lighthouses and other aids to navigation, including lighthouses, light vessels, buoys, beacons, seamarks, supplies, and related records, for use by the United States. It also gives the Secretary of Commerce, through the Commissioner of Lighthouses, the administrative duties for this lighthouse service. The Secretary must have estimates prepared and sent to Congress for money to cover the cost of setting up and maintaining these aids to navigation.

2664.s: This order gives the United States Shipping Board Emergency Fleet Corporation the President’s powers under the Emergency Shipping Fund section for building vessels, buying or taking vessels under construction, and getting materials for ship construction. It also gives the United States Shipping Board those powers for taking title or possession of built vessels or parts of them, as well as charters, and for operating, managing, and disposing of those vessels. The board may use these powers itself or through the Emergency Fleet Corporation or another corporation it creates for that purpose.

2653.s: This order takes over the cargo steamship Prinz Eitel Friedrich for the United States. It gives the United States Shipping Board control of the vessel and lets it repair, equip, man, operate, lease, or charter it in U.S. service or commerce. The Secretary of the Navy must appoint a board to find the vessel's actual value, and that report can be used in claims for compensation.

2645.s: This order gives the Secretary of Commerce control over carrying out presidential instructions and proclamations under Title VII. It also lets the secretary grant or refuse export licenses under those instructions. The order creates an Exports Council made up of the Secretary of State, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of Commerce, and the Food Administrator. The council is directed to make policy recommendations for the President to help carry out the act.

2651.s: This order takes over the possession and title of the listed vessels that were owned by Germany or by German citizens or subjects. It directs the United States Shipping Board to repair, equip, and man those vessels. The board may also operate, lease, or charter them in U.S. service or in foreign or coastwise commerce.

2641.s: This order amends the Alaskan Railroad Townsite Regulations. It removes the rule that lots could be forfeited for using them to make or sell intoxicating liquors as a beverage, for gambling, prostitution, or other unlawful purposes. It also says no lot can be forfeited for violating those provisions.

2635.s: This order takes immediate possession and title of the German vessel Staatssekretar Solf for the United States. It directs the Secretary of the Navy to operate and equip the vessel in the service of the Navy of the United States until further directions.

2628.s: This order lets the Civil Service Commission, if it thinks it is in the service’s interest, allow the War Department to hire inspection staff from British, French, Russian, or Italian government munitions factories in this country during the present war. The War Department must give the Commission a list of each person’s name, job title, pay rate, and nationality when it asks for this authority.

2626.s: This order changes Civil Service Rule IX on when people who left competitive service jobs can be reinstated. It allows reinstatement for a person who left without delinquency or misconduct, if the separation was within the stated time limit and any required examination is passed. It also allows a person who left a scientific, professional, or technical competitive job to serve a State, county, municipality, or foreign government in a similar job to be reinstated after that service, if the required certificate is issued.

2625.s: The order directs the Secretary of the Treasury to transfer several German vessels to the Navy. The Navy is to use them as colliers and cargo carriers.

2624.s: This order takes immediate possession and title of four German vessels and places them under the United States through the Secretary of the Navy. It also orders the Secretary of the Navy to operate and equip those vessels for service in the Navy of the United States until further directions.

2621.s: The order directs the Secretary of the Treasury to transfer the German vessel Atlas, now at San Francisco, to the commandant of the twelfth naval district. The ship is to be used for harbor patrol.

2619-A.s: The order takes immediate possession and title of the German vessels Odenwald and Praesident, which are in the harbor of San Juan, Puerto Rico. It also directs the Secretary of the Navy to operate and equip the ships for service in the United States Navy until further directions.

2617.s: The order lets the Civil Service Commission allow civilian employees attached to military organizations sent to Europe to be appointed without following the Civil Service Law and Rules. It affects civilian employees attached to those military organizations.

2612.s: This order reserves certain lands in Arizona from disposal and sets them aside temporarily. The land is to be used until allotments can be made to the Navajo Indians living there, or until another provision can be made for their welfare. The reservation is subject to all prior valid rights and claims, and to earlier water-power designations and power-site reserves.

2605-A.s: This order takes over radio stations in the United States that are needed for Naval Communications and puts them under government control. It also lets the government close other radio stations that are not needed for those communications and remove the radio equipment from them. The Secretary of the Navy is directed to carry out the order.

2605.s: This order suspends the Eight-Hour Act for certain contracts with the War Department for military buildings and other public work the Secretary of War says is important for national defense. It says laborers and mechanics on that work may be required to work more than eight hours a day when the Secretary of War decides it is necessary for national defense. It applies during the emergency or until another order changes it.

2604.s: This order prohibits companies and other people who own or operate telegraph and telephone lines or submarine cables from sending messages to places outside the United States. It also blocks them from delivering messages received from those places, unless the messages are allowed under rules set by the Secretary of War or the Secretary of the Navy. It applies to telegraph and telephone lines and to submarine cables.

2602.s: This order says state, county, and municipal civil service commissions may work with the United States Civil Service Commission to help meet Federal Government hiring needs in the civil service. The United States Civil Service Commission may use an eligible register from one of those commissions if it agrees and if the examinations meet the required standards. People on those eligible lists may be certified and appointed as if they had passed the federal examination, and they get the same rights and privileges.

2600.s: The Council of National Defense is allowed to hire people for the period of the war without following the civil service law and rules. The people in charge may choose workers they think are best suited for the work. The order says the Civil Service Commission’s registers should still be used as much as possible.

2594.s: This order creates a Committee on Public Information. It puts the Secretary of State, the Secretary of War, the Secretary of the Navy, and a civilian in charge of it. It names George Creel as the civilian chairman and allows the three secretaries to assign officers to work for the committee.

2596.s: This order waives a rule that had barred Federal employees from holding office under a State, territorial, or municipal government. It lets employees in and under the Treasury Department, with approval from the Secretary of the Treasury, serve on State, county, or municipal councils or committees of defense. The service is for mobilizing and conserving the resources of the country.

2585.s: This order says radio stations needed for naval communications are to be taken over by the U.S. Government and used under its control. It also says other radio stations that are not needed for naval communications may be closed. It affects radio stations within the United States and puts enforcement in the hands of the Secretary of the Navy.

2587-A.s: This order lets the head of a department or independent office remove a federal employee if there is reason to believe the person’s conduct, sympathies, or statements would be harmful to the public welfare, or for other war-related reasons. The removal can be done without other formal steps, but the reasons must be kept as a confidential record. The record is still open to inspection by the Civil Service Commission.

2570.s: This order tells the Civil Service Commission to refuse exams or certification for people who are now working in government service or who worked there within the past three months, unless their department or office gives written permission. That permission must be based on whether the person can do better service for the Government in the job being tested for. The order says it was issued because of the present international situation and will be withdrawn when the emergency is over.

2572.s: This order temporarily suspends the law that limits some Department of Agriculture contract work to eight hours a day. It applies to people working under contract with the Department of Agriculture, and it says their wages must still be figured on an eight-hour basic day with overtime at not less than time and one-half for hours over eight.

2549.s: This order withdraws certain lands in New Mexico from entry, sale, or other disposition. It sets those lands apart as a reservation for the use and occupancy of the Indians of the Laguna Pueblo and other Pueblo Indians the Secretary of the Interior may settle there. The order does not apply to tracts where title has passed out of the United States or where valid legal rights have already attached.

2569-A.s: This order sets up open competitive exams for vacancies in postmaster jobs in first-, second-, and third-class post offices. When a vacancy happens, the Civil Service Commission rates the applicants and sends the result to the Postmaster General, who then submits the highest qualified eligible person for appointment unless that person is disqualified by character or residence. People who have passed their sixty-fifth birthday are not given the exam.

2537.s: This order withdraws certain United States lands in Alaska from settlement, location, sale, or entry. It reserves those lands for the Navy Department to use as a distant control receiving station with the naval radio station near Cordova, Alaska. The land covered is within one-fourth of a mile of a specified point on the Copper River and Northwestern Railroad, on the left side of the tracks traveling from Cordova.

2533.s: This order withdraws a tract of land in Alaska from settlement, location, sale, entry, or other disposition. It reserves the land for use by the U.S. Navy Department as a Naval Radio Station.

2524.s: This order revokes earlier withdrawals of certain lands in Arizona that had been set aside for the Papago Indians. It then withdraws and sets apart a listed area in Arizona as a reservation for the benefit of the Papago Indians, while keeping tribal rights to the minerals in the land. Mineral lands in the reservation can still be explored, located, and entered under existing mining laws, and existing legal rights to the land are not affected.

2526.s: This order says Chinese persons may not enter or remain in the Canal Zone, except as allowed in the order. It also sets rules for ship masters to report Chinese persons on board and limits when they may land. Some Chinese diplomats, residents, workers under contract, and others named in the order are excepted. Violations can bring a fine, jail, or both.

2505.s: This order extends, for one year, the trust or other restriction on selling land in any patent issued to an Indian for lands on the public domain, if that restriction would otherwise end during 1917. It does not apply to the named Indian homesteaders listed in the order.

2479.s: This order requires deposit money orders issued by the Canal Zone Postal Service to earn interest at a set rate for each three-month period. Interest is paid when the order is paid, and it does not build up for more than three years. It also lets the Governor of The Panama Canal make rules to carry out the order.

2462.s: This order changes the rules for invoices for merchandise priced in depreciated currency. It requires a currency certificate to be attached showing the amount of depreciation compared with standard coin currency and the value in standard coin currency. The certificate is used when duty is assessed, and it is also required for statistical purposes on all such invoices.

2456.s: The order says the Governor General of the Philippine Islands must make official reports to the War Department. It also places matters about the government of the Philippine Islands under that department’s jurisdiction, except where law says otherwise, and assigns the War Department’s civil government work there to the Bureau of Insular Affairs.

2461.s: The order directs principal consular officers to keep a register of American citizens living in their districts and to invite resident Americans to have their names entered. It says applications must be approved by the Department, and the register must include personal and family information and proof of citizenship. Consuls may issue one-year certificates of registration for use with local authorities, but people with unexpired passports cannot get them except in an emergency authorized by the Department. A $1 fee is required only for the certificate of registration.

2418.s: This order sets rules for selling lots in the Federal and Cliff Additions to the townsite of Seward, Alaska. It says the lots must be sold under earlier sale regulations, with new rules for the sale price, cash payments, use restrictions, and forfeiture if the buyer does not meet the payment terms. It also sets when entry and patent papers can be issued.

2413.s: This order waives the United States citizenship requirement so Cedric R. Landon can be certified for appointment as a predatory animal inspector in the Bureau of Biological Survey in Texas. It applies to Mr. Landon, who was born in Canada, declared his intention to become a U.S. citizen, and had been serving temporarily in that job. He had passed the examination, but could not be certified under the existing rules.

2375.s: This order permanently withdraws a 40-acre tract in California from settlement, location, entry, sale, or other disposal. It reserves the land as an addition to the reservation for the Camp or Fort Independence Indians, subject to any valid existing rights.

2345.s: This order increases the enlisted strength of the Regular Army within the continental United States up to the statutory maximum. It applies to the arms of service listed, including Infantry, Cavalry, Field Artillery, Coast Artillery Corps, and Engineers.

2332.s: This order revokes earlier orders that had temporarily withdrawn lands in the former Siletz Indian Reservation in Oregon. It says the unappropriated lands will be open to entry under the act of August 15, 1894, on and after April 1, 1916.

2341.s: The order lets the Secretary of the Treasury direct customs officers to take up passports from American citizens returning to the United States. Passports that will not be used again may be canceled and returned to the owners. Passports that will be used again are sent to the Department of State, and the owners must notify that department before leaving again. If a person plans to travel for a different purpose or to a country not listed in the passport, they must apply for a new passport.

2326.s: This order extends by one year the trust or other restriction on selling or transferring certain patents issued to any Indian for a homestead on the public domain. It applies to cases where that restriction would otherwise expire during 1916, except for the specific homesteaders listed in the order.

2285.s: The order directs the State Department and Treasury to inspect passports of all people leaving the United States, whether American or foreign. It says American citizens applying for passports must file duplicate applications with three copies of a photograph. They must also tell the State Department where they plan to leave, what date they will depart, and what ship they will use if they sail from an American port.

2273.s: This order changes the southern boundary of the Colorado River Indian Reservation in Arizona. It says the earlier survey placed that boundary in the wrong place and sets a new boundary line based on surveyed markers and section lines. This affects the reservation land and the boundary used for it.

2269.s: This order suspends part of a law about American seamen in the merchant marine. It pauses the rules in section 4488 of the Revised Statutes until September 3, 1916. This affects American seamen covered by that law.

2268.s: This order withdraws certain areas in Idaho for use by the Department of Agriculture as a sheep-breeding and grazing experimental station. It does not apply to lands covered by valid adverse claims that were made before the order and kept under law.

2262.s: This order amends consular rules for American sailors on foreign voyages and in foreign ports. It covers what masters must do when sailors desert, how crew lists and bonds are handled, when sailors may be discharged, and when consular officers must collect wages and extra wages. It also sets rules for wages, wage allotments, no advance wages, and care for sailors who are injured or sick.

2223.s: This order changes an earlier order that had temporarily withdrawn public lands within the former Siletz Indian Reservation in Oregon for classification and pending legislation. It excludes lands within the Siuslaw National Forest from that withdrawal. It also says it does not change or revoke the earlier proclamation or Executive Order No. 860.

2185.s: This order renames the part of the Panama Canal through the continental divide from “Culebra Cut” to “Gaillard Cut.” It applies to that part of the canal and changes the name used for it. The order says the new name honors Lieutenant-Colonel D. D. Gaillard of the United States Army Corps of Engineers, who was in charge of work there until near completion.

2138.s: The order reserves 640 acres in Arizona for military use by the National Guard of Arizona as a rifle range. It also releases another parcel from a previous military reservation. That land returns to its former status as part of the Navajo Indian Reservation in Arizona.

2133.s: This order extends by one year the trust or other restriction on selling certain lands on the public domain that were patented to Indians. It applies in cases where that restriction would otherwise end during 1915.

2060.s: This order withdraws certain lands in the Territory of Alaska from settlement, location, sale, entry, and other disposition. It reserves those lands for townsite purposes.

2052.s: This order changes the rules for injury compensation paid to employees of The Panama Canal and the Panama Railroad Company. It allows payment to certain dependent relatives of a deceased employee, including a parent, brother, sister, grandparent, or grandchild. The total paid to all beneficiaries cannot be more than half of the employee’s monthly pay, and payments can end if the relative dies, marries, or becomes able to support himself or herself.

2067.s: This order temporarily withdraws 40 acres in Idaho from settlement, location, sale, or entry, except as allowed by the cited laws. It reserves the land for use by the Forest Service as an addition to a ranger station for administration of the Caribou National Forest.

2051.s: This order changes the law against gambling in the Canal Zone. It says a person who plays for money or bets money or property on gambling games or devices can be fined up to $100, jailed up to 30 days, or both. It applies to people within the Canal Zone.

2048.s: This order revokes the withdrawal of about 40 acres of unsurveyed land in Oregon that had been reserved as a ranger station for the Forest Service. The land was being used in connection with the administration of the Oregon National Forest.

2046.s: This order temporarily withdraws 80 acres from settlement, location, sale, or entry, except as allowed by the named laws. It reserves the land for use by the Forest Service as a ranger station for administering the Coconino National Forest.

2047.s: This order temporarily withdraws certain public lands in Wyoming so the Department of Agriculture may select land there for use as an elk refuge. It also revokes part of a 1913 executive order that covered a nearby section of land.

2045.s: This order transfers the lands in the Zuni National Forest to the Manzano National Forest. It merges the Zuni and Manzano lands into one national forest, to be known as the Manzano National Forest, and changes its boundaries. It does not add any other lands to the Manzano National Forest or release any lands from national forest reservation.

2044.s: This order allows William C. DeLanoy to be appointed Director and J. Brooks B. Parker to be appointed Assistant to the Director in the Bureau of War Risk Insurance in the Treasury Department without following Civil Service rules. It says these jobs need specially qualified people because of the technical work in the new bureau.

2039.s: This order lets foreign-built ships admitted to United States registry keep their watch officers without regard to citizenship for seven years. It also says those watch officers may be promoted, and vacancies in the first two years may be filled without regard to citizenship. For two years, the usual rules for survey, inspection, and measurement of these ships by United States officers are suspended.

2042.s: This order takes over one or more high-powered radio stations in the United States that can communicate across the Atlantic. The government will use or control them exclusively for communication with land stations in Europe, including code and cipher messages. The Secretary of the Navy is directed to enforce the order and make regulations for it.

2031.s: This order renames the present Customs Collection Districts by number and lists the new numbered districts. It applies to customs districts across many states and territories, including places such as Maine and New Hampshire, New York, California, Alaska, Hawaii, and Porto Rico.

2030.s: This order changes a prior order that added public land to the Gila River Reservation in Arizona. It removes the south half of the northwest quarter of section 10, township 5 south, range 8 east of the Gila and Salt River meridian from that added land.

2029.s: This order transfers a 6-acre part of the Military Reservation of Deadmans Island at Los Angeles harbor, California, to the Treasury Department. It sets that land aside for use by the Public Health Service.

2024.s: This order temporarily withdraws 160 acres of land from settlement, location, sale, or entry, except as allowed by the cited laws. It reserves the land for use by the Forest Service as a lookout station for the administration of the Colorado National Forest.

2023.s: This order withdraws a described parcel of land in California from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposition. It sets the land aside for Indian use, subject to any valid existing rights.

2022.s: This order waives fees for emergency passports and for the work done to apply for them. It also waives fees for visaing passports by diplomatic or consular officers, and says no visa may be attached after a passport has expired. The order does not change fees already collected before officers received notice, and the Secretary of State may end the waiver later.

2021.s: The Secretary of State is allowed, at his discretion, to issue passports to American citizens abroad in cases of urgent necessity. Applications can be made in their behalf by near relatives or legal representatives in this country.

2020.s: This order changes maritime quarantine rules for the Panama Canal Zone and the harbors of Panama and Colon. It updates health certificate forms, says some vessels do not need a new bill of health if they carry extra copies from a foreign port, and adds rules for baggage, inspection, quarantine, and penalties. It also says vessels or people may be held in quarantine if they could carry diseases such as plague, yellow fever, cholera, smallpox, typhus fever, or leprosy.

2019.s:
This order lets a defendant or court officer ask a plaintiff in a civil case or special proceeding to give security for costs. If the plaintiff does not provide the required security, the case may be dismissed.
It applies in the district court and magistrates' courts in the Canal Zone, and it also covers intervenors and defendants making counterclaims after ending their own suit. The United States, The Panama Canal, the Canal Zone Government, and some court-appointed fiduciaries do not have to give security for costs.

2018.s: This order extends the United States Postal Laws and Regulations that define crimes against the Postal Service to the Canal Zone, except where they are not locally applicable. It makes those laws enforceable in the Canal Zone courts like other criminal cases.

2017.s: This order says the Treasury Department will issue all instructions to customs officers about enforcing the United States neutrality laws. It applies until changed by later direction and is meant to make enforcement more prompt and effective during the emergency conditions then existing.

2016.s: This order sets customs rules for ships arriving in the Canal Zone from foreign ports. It requires ship masters to show the ship’s manifest and give a true account of the vessel’s destination, or face fines. Goods not listed on the manifest, and certain sea stores not properly listed or landed without a permit, can be seized and forfeited, and the master can be fined. Customs officers are also authorized to administer oaths and certify invoices for shipments from the Canal Zone to the United States.

2013.s: This order creates a Board of Relief made up of the Secretaries of State, the Treasury, War, and the Navy. The board will oversee the work for the relief, protection, and transportation of American citizens abroad, and the Secretary of the Treasury will serve as chairman.

2012.s: This order directs the State, Treasury, War, and Navy departments to work together on relief, protection, and transportation for American citizens abroad because of disturbed conditions in Europe. It calls for Navy ships to carry relief workers, supplies, and money to selected ports. It also tells the War Department to organize relief and transport refugees, and the Treasury and State departments to handle funds and gather and share information.

2011.s: This order prohibits all radio stations within the United States from sending or receiving messages of an unneutral nature for delivery. It also bars them from giving any unneutral service to any of the belligerents during the hostilities. The Secretary of the Navy is directed to enforce the order.

2006.s: The order sets apart land in the Canal Zone for a radio station and other naval purposes under the control of the Secretary of the Navy. The area is called the Darien Naval Radio Station. It remains subject to the civil jurisdiction of the Canal Zone authorities under the Panama Canal Act.

1999.s: This order says returns for corporations, joint stock companies, associations, and insurance companies may be inspected only under rules set by the Secretary of the Treasury and approved by the President. It also says proper officers of a state with a general income tax may get access to those returns, or an abstract of them, if the governor requests it and the Treasury rules allow it.

1997.s: This order changes the civil service rules for filling vacancies. If an examination is announced and there are not enough citizen eligibles, the Commission may examine people who are not citizens. They still cannot be certified for appointment while citizens are eligible.

1995.s: This order changes earlier orders that had set aside certain Arizona townships as additions to the Navajo Indian Reservation. It releases unappropriated land in one section of Arizona and reserves it as a rifle range for Company G, First Infantry, Organized Militia of the State of Arizona. If the land is no longer used or needed for that purpose, it will return to its former status as an Indian reservation.

1959.s: This order sets aside Smith and Minor Islands for the Department of Agriculture to use as a preserve, breeding ground, and winter sanctuary for native birds. It also says the islands will still be used for lighthouse purposes and that this use will not be interfered with. It makes it unlawful to hunt, trap, capture, disturb, or kill any bird there, or to take bird eggs, unless allowed under rules set by the Secretary of Agriculture.

1944.s: This order creates a six-member committee to arrange and provide ceremonies for the official opening of the Panama Canal. The committee must be made up of former members of the Isthmian Canal Commission and works under the direction of the Governor of the Panama Canal. It also sets pay, travel, and other approved expenses for the committee members and allows spending for printing, postage, correspondence, clerks, and other needed costs.

1926.s: This order changes the rules for pay for consuls-general and consuls who receive salaries fixed by law. It says their salary can cover time spent getting instructions, traveling to their posts, and serving at their posts, under set limits. It also says no salary allowance is made in some cases unless the officer is actually in transit to the post or receiving instructions as directed.

1888.s: This order sets employment rules for workers on the Panama Canal and related operations. It covers pay, hiring rules, transfers, hours, transportation, housing, medical care, and leave. It also gives the Governor of the Panama Canal power to make appointments, set regulations, and discharge employees for cause.

1885.s: This order creates a permanent organization for the Panama Canal and the Canal Zone. It sets up departments for operation and maintenance, purchasing, supply, accounting, health, and executive administration, all under the Governor and subject to the Secretary of War. It also says the new organization takes effect on April 1, 1914, and the Isthmian Canal Commission and the present Panama Canal organization will then cease to exist.

1884.s: This order makes it a misdemeanor in the Canal Zone to hunt at night with a lantern, torch, bonfire, or other artificial light. It also forbids hunting with a gun or other firearm set off by an animal or bird, or by a spring, trap, or similar mechanical device. The order also repeals a 1909 executive order.

1864.s: This order reserves a fractional section in New Mexico from all forms of entry or other disposal. It sets the land aside for administration purposes connected with the San Juan Indian boarding school on the Navajo Reservation. It also changes a 1910 coal land withdrawal to remove that section from it.

1880.s: This order makes it unlawful in the Canal Zone to give, offer, or promise gifts or gratuities to an agent, employee, or servant without the knowledge and consent of the person they work for if the goal is to influence their actions. It also bars those workers from asking for or taking gifts, commissions, discounts, or bonuses in connection with their employer’s business without that consent. Violations can bring a fine, jail time, or both.

1857.s: This order sets rules for carrying firearms and other listed weapons in the Canal Zone. It says people who carry them without permission can be fined or jailed, and the weapons can be seized and confiscated. It does not apply to certain military, peace officer, mail, fund-carrying, and approved gun or pistol club members, and it allows permits for hunting and for keeping arms in homes, offices, business places, plantations, and for watchmen or overseers.

1860.s: This order sets rules for interest on money in the Canal Zone. It says interest cannot be more than six percent a year unless the agreement is in writing, and then it cannot be more than twelve percent a year. Contracts that break this rule are void as to the interest, and people who paid too much interest may recover it in court within two years. It also says no evidence of usury may be used unless it is pleaded and verified by affidavit.

1798.s: This order revokes Executive Order No. 1540. That earlier order had reserved certain tracts of land in Arizona from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposition for use of the Walapai Indians.

1819.s: The order sets apart Anaho Island for the Department of Agriculture to use as a preserve and breeding ground for native birds. It makes it unlawful for anyone to hunt, trap, capture, disturb, or kill birds there, or take their eggs, unless allowed under rules set by the Secretary of Agriculture. It applies to anyone on the reserve.

1782.s: This order withdraws certain lands in Arizona from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposal. It sets those lands aside as an addition to the Gila River Indian Reservation in Arizona. Any existing valid rights to those lands are still protected.

1786.s: This order temporarily withdraws certain public lands in Township 41 North, Range 2 West, in Arizona from settlement, location, sale, or entry. It does this so the lands can be classified and while legislation is pending for their proper disposition. It does not change departmental orders that include part of those lands within the Kaibab Indian Reservation.

1772.s: This order withdraws certain land in Nevada County, California, from entry, sale, or other disposition. It sets the land aside for the Nevada or Colony tribe of Indians living near Nevada City, California. It says any valid existing rights of any person are not affected.

1774.s: The order withdraws a section of land in New Mexico from settlement, entry, or other disposal. It sets the land aside for use of Navajo Indians living near Crownpoint, subject to any prior valid rights or claims and to another coal land withdrawal.

1699.s: This order withdraws certain lands in Arizona from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposition. It sets the lands aside for use of Navajo Indians, while keeping any prior valid existing rights in the land.

1700.s: This order withdraws a specific piece of land in New Mexico from settlement and entry. It sets the land apart as a reservation for use of the Navajo Indians in common, while keeping any valid prior rights to the land.

1682.s: This order withdraws 40 acres in Montana from entry and sets it apart for administrative purposes connected with the affairs of the Flathead Indians. It says the withdrawal does not affect any valid prior rights to the land.

1681.s: This order withdraws certain lands in Nevada from entry, sale, or other disposal. It sets the lands aside for Paiute and Shoshoni Indians, and for other Indians the Secretary of the Interior may settle there. Any prior valid rights to the land are not affected.

1655.s: This order restores certain lands in Arizona that had been reserved for use of the Papago Indians to the public domain. In their place, it withdraws three new tracts of land from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposition. These lands are reserved for school, agency, and other necessary uses for the benefit of Papago or other Indians in the state.

1649.s: This order cancels a previous order that added land to the Moapa River Indian reservation in Nevada. It sets aside 128.37 acres as an addition to the reservation and keeps the land from settlement, sale, or other disposition. The withdrawal is subject to any prior valid rights in the land.

1632.s: This order sets aside 89.70 acres in Nevada as an addition to the Moapa River Indian Reservation. The land is reserved from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposition, but any prior valid rights to the land are not affected.

1621.s: This order changes two earlier orders about land in Arizona connected to the Papago Indians reservation. It removes the south half of Section 13 from one order and revokes another order that had taken the south half of Section 15 out of withdrawal for Indian purposes.

1606.s: This order reserves certain land in Nevada from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposal. It sets that land aside for Indian allotment purposes, while keeping any prior valid existing rights of other persons.

1598.s: This order amends a prior order to remove certain lands from reservation for the Maricopa band or village of Papago Indians. The lands listed are in Arizona, south and east of the Gila and Salt River principal meridian.

1603.s: This order temporarily reserves certain lands in California from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposition. It does this while their suitableness for allotment purposes to homeless Paiute or other Indians living on or adjacent to the land is investigated. Any tracts already occupied and improved by a person and listed under the Act of June 11, 1906 are excepted.

1579.s: This order withdraws most of the lands in the Fort Duchesne military reservation in Utah from military use and places them under the full control of the Department of the Interior. It keeps 150 acres in reservation for military purposes, including the buildings of the post of Fort Duchesne.

1558.s: This order reserves two tracts of land in Tripp County, South Dakota, from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposal. The land is set aside for Indian school and administrative purposes, but it remains subject to any prior valid rights of any persons.

1522.s: This order withdraws a described parcel of land in California from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposition. It reserves the land for Indian use, while keeping any valid existing rights of any person to it.

1529.s: This order temporarily reserves certain lands in California from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposition. The land is to be investigated for whether it is suitable for allotment purposes to homeless Paiute or other Indians living on or near it. The reservation does not affect certain rights of way or any prior legal use of the land, and it does not apply to tracts already occupied and improved by a person under the stated law.

1518.s: This order withdraws a specific parcel of land in the Flathead Indian Reservation in Montana from settlement, location, sale, and entry. The land is reserved for examination and classification, subject to the conditions in the act of June 25, 1910.

1517.s: This order sets aside two parcels of land in California for Indian use. It says the land is reserved from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposal, but is still subject to any prior valid existing claim.

1496.s: This order reserves certain lands in California from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposal. It sets the lands aside for allotment purposes for the Indians living there and for other lawful uses for their benefit. It does not affect prior legal uses of the land for public purposes, and it excepts occupied and improved tracts listed under the Act of June 11, 1906.

1495.s: The order reserves an unsurveyed island in the Pacific Ocean near the mouth of Smith River in California from all forms of disposal. It sets the island aside for use of the Smith River Indians and for any other purposes the Secretary of the Interior may direct or authorize. The order is subject to any prior valid existing rights of any persons.

1485.s: This order changes earlier orders that had reserved certain lands in California for Indian purposes. It restores the listed tracts to the public domain so they can be used for settlement and entry.

1483.s: This order restores certain lands in New Mexico to the status they had before they were removed from the Navajo reservation. It says this is to allow an exchange of lands to be completed and for allotment to the Indians. After that, any remaining lands may be opened for disposition by the Secretary of the Interior with notice as he prescribes.

1482.s: This order changes the boundaries of the Zuni National Forest in Arizona and New Mexico. It removes parts of the Zuni and Navajo Indian Reservations from the forest, while keeping some Navajo land as national forest land. It restores the Zuni Reservation and part of the Navajo Reservation to the status they had before the 1909 proclamation, except for the land kept as forest.

1481.s: This order changes the boundaries of the Alamo National Forest in New Mexico by removing the part of the Mescalero Apache Indian Reservation that had been included in the forest. It restores the reservation to the status it had before that land was added to the forest. This affects the Mescalero Apache Indian Reservation and the Alamo National Forest.

1480.s: This order changes the boundaries of the Trinity National Forest by taking out all of the Hoopa Valley Indian Reservation land that had been included in it. It restores the Hoopa Valley Indian Reservation to the status it had before that earlier inclusion. The reservation is fully recreated and restored to that earlier status.

1479.s: This order removes part of the White Mountain Apache Indian Reservation from the Sitgreaves National Forest in Arizona. It restores the reservation to the status it had before it was included in the forest. The change affects the land in the reservation and the forest boundary.

1478.s: This order changes the boundaries of Sequoia National Forest to remove the part of the Tule River Indian Reservation that was included in the forest. It restores that reservation to the status it had before the 1909 proclamation, as if the land had not been added to the forest. This affects the Tule River Indian Reservation and the land covered by the forest boundary change.

1477.s: This order changes the boundaries of the Crook National Forest in Arizona by taking out part of the White Mountain Apache Indian Reservation. It restores that land to the reservation and puts it back in the status it had before March 2, 1909.

1476.s: This order removes part of the Jicarilla Apache Indian Reservation from the Carson National Forest in New Mexico. It restores the reservation to the status it had before it was included in the forest. The change applies to the land covered by the earlier forest proclamation.

1465.s: This order sets aside a specific area in Tooele County, Utah, and keeps it from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposal. It reserves the land for school, agency, and other necessary uses for the benefit of Indians on the public domain in Utah, while still subject to any valid existing rights.

1475.s: This order changes the boundaries of the Apache National Forest by taking out land that was part of the White Mountain Apache Indian Reservation. It restores that reservation to the status it had before the 1909 order that put those lands into the forest.

1447.s: This order temporarily withdraws all of township 5 south, range 7 east in Arizona from settlement, location, sale, or entry. It does not apply to parts of that township that had already been reserved and set aside as an addition to the Gila River Indian Reservation, and the land is reserved for classification.

1426.s: This order changes an earlier land withdrawal in Arizona to make part of section 35 permanently unavailable for settlement, entry, sale, or other disposition. The land is to be used for the Pima and Maricopa Indians, and for other Indians the Secretary of the Interior chooses to settle there. Existing valid rights of any persons to the land are still protected.

1416.s: This order changes an earlier order to permanently withdraw certain land in Arizona south of the Salt River from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposition. The land is for the use of the Pima and Maricopa Indians, and the Secretary of the Interior may also settle other Indians there, subject to existing valid rights.

1406.s: This order changes an earlier order about land in New Mexico for the Indians of the Jemez Pueblo. It withdraws the land from sale and settlement and sets it apart as a reservation for their use and benefit, except for land that has already left U.S. ownership or has valid legal rights attached to it.

1379.s: This order withdraws certain lands in Florida from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposal. It sets those lands aside as a reservation for the Seminole Indians in southern Florida. The withdrawal is subject to any existing valid rights or claims of any persons.

1387.s: The order reserves certain lands in Pinal County, Arizona, from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposal. It adds those lands to the Gila River Indian Reservation. The reservation is subject to any valid existing rights of other persons.

1368.s: The order reserves a described piece of land in Arizona from entry, sale, settlement, or other disposition. It sets the land aside for use of the Walapai Indians, while keeping any valid existing rights to the land.

1374.s: This order reserves certain lands in Pima County, Arizona, from settlement, entry, sale, or other disposal. The lands are set aside for school, agency, and other necessary uses for the benefit of the Papago Indians, subject to any valid existing rights.

1349.s: This order changes the earlier reservation set aside for the Pima and Maricopa Indians. It makes the reservation available for the Pima and Maricopa Indians and for other Indians the Secretary of the Interior chooses to settle there.

1359.s: This order reserves certain lands in New Mexico for Indian purposes. It bars those lands from entry, sale, or other disposition. It also says valid existing rights of any person are not affected.

1322.s: This order changes the 1879 reservation order for the Pima and Maricopa Indians. It makes the reservation available for use by the Pima and Maricopa Indians and by other Indians that the Secretary of the Interior chooses to settle there.

1301.s: This order says Article 7 of the 1854 treaty will no longer apply across most of the land ceded by the Chippewa Indians of Lake Superior to the United States. It keeps that article in force in a specified part of that territory and in all of Minnesota east of the 4th Principal Meridian until the President changes it.

1299.s: This order says the land ceded by the Treaty of August 21, 1847 will no longer be held by the United States as Indian land. It affects the country ceded under that treaty.

1300.s: This order changes how Article 7 of the 1863 treaty applies in the territory ceded by the Red Lake and Pembina Bands of Chippewa Indians. It stops that article from applying in most of the ceded land, but it stays in force in the part east of the 6th Guide Meridian until Congress or the President changes it.

1296.s: This order cancels a prior order that had added land to the Fort Mojave Indian Reservation. It withdraws the listed lands in Arizona from settlement and entry and sets them apart as an addition to the reservation. The land is for the use and occupation of the Fort Mojave and other Indians the Secretary of the Interior chooses, and it does not affect any existing valid rights to the land.

1284.s: This order restores to the public domain all lands in certain New Mexico townships that were added to the Navajo Reservation by earlier executive orders, if those lands were not allotted to Indians or otherwise reserved. It affects lands lying west of the first guide meridian west.

1267.s: This order withdraws certain lands in Arizona from settlement and entry and adds them to the Fort Mojave Indian Reservation. The land is set apart for the use and occupation of the Fort Mojave and other Indians the Secretary of the Interior chooses to settle there. It does not affect any existing valid rights to the land.

1271.s: This order withdraws a described parcel of land in Idaho from settlement, entry, and sale. It sets the land apart as an addition to the Indian school and agency site on the Coeur d'Alene Reservation until it is no longer needed for that purpose. It also says existing valid rights to the land are not affected.

1256.s: The order withdraws certain lands in Arizona from settlement, entry, and sale and sets them apart as an addition to the Salt River Indian Reservation. It says any existing valid rights to those lands are not affected.

1224.s: This order revokes part of a 1877 executive order that had set aside certain land in California for Indian purposes. The revocation applies to the south half of section 20, township 3 south, range 1 east of the San Bernardino meridian.

1221.s: This order sets aside a described tract of land in New Mexico as a reservation for the use and occupation of the Pueblo Indians belonging to the Pueblo Laguna. It also says the order does not affect any existing valid rights of any person to the lands described.

1220.s: This order withdraws certain lands in Idaho from settlement, entry, and sale. It sets those lands apart as an addition to the Duck Valley Indian Reservation. It also says any existing valid rights to the lands are not affected.

1216.s: This order reserves 5 acres of unsurveyed land in Beaverhead County, Montana, for military purposes. The land is to be used to protect the Big Hole Battlefield Monument.

1172.s: The order restores certain lands within the Mescalero Apache Indian Reservation in New Mexico to the public domain. It applies to the lands covered by small holdings claims Nos. 484 and 486 as shown in the records of the General Land Office and the attached blue print.

1143.s: This order sets rules for appointments, promotions, transfers, and retention in the diplomatic service and the Department of State. It requires efficiency records, sets examinations for many diplomatic appointments, and limits outside appointments to lower secretary grades unless there is a vacancy in a higher grade. It also says promotions and appointments should be based on efficiency and ability, not political affiliation, and it keeps records to guide promotion or retention of clerks and other officers.

1142.s: This order bars government bureau, office, and division chiefs and their subordinates from asking Congress for legislation, appropriations, or other congressional action unless the department head knows and consents. It also bars Army, Navy, and Marine Corps officers stationed in Washington from doing the same. These officials also may not answer requests from Congress unless the department head authorizes it.

1135.s: This order restores a parcel of land in Washington to the public domain. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to allot that land to Perry Yukton, an enrolled member of the Chehalis Tribe, under the cited law.

1121.s: This order changes the Civil Service Rules to allow six special agents of the General Land Office to be listed in Schedule A. These agents investigate fraudulent entries and other criminal matters in the Interior Department. It affects the General Land Office special agents named in the rule.

1120.s: This order extends the time for the Spanish Treaty Claims Commission to keep its powers and jurisdiction for six more months, starting on September 2, 1909. The commission was appointed to examine and decide claims of citizens of the United States against Spain. The extension is only for that work and no longer.

1116.s: This order gives certain convicts in the Canal Zone penitentiary time off their sentences if they have no recorded rule violations and do their assigned duties in a faithful, orderly, and peaceable way. It sets the amount of time that can be taken off based on how long they have served. If a convict breaks the rules or laws, the order lets time off be taken away, and the chief executive of the Canal Zone may restore lost time.

1115.s: This order changes the Canal Zone law on penalties for murder. It says a person guilty of murder in the first degree shall suffer death, or life in the penitentiary if there are extenuating circumstances. It also says a person guilty of murder in the second degree is punishable by imprisonment in the penitentiary for not less than ten years.

1113.s: This order changes rules for communications to the Department of State. It says despatches should be addressed to the Secretary of State and written in a set format. It also says secret or reserved despatches should be marked "Confidential," and private letters about official consulate business are disapproved.

1092.s: This order says that if the Secretary, First Assistant Secretary, and Assistant Secretary of the Interior Department are all absent, the Assistant Attorney-General for the Interior Department will serve as Acting Secretary. It affects the Interior Department and sets who takes over its duties in that situation.

1110.s: The order says reports that the governor or executive council of Porto Rico must make to U.S. officials will now go to the War Department. It also puts matters about the government of Porto Rico under that department. If the next year’s support funds are not approved, the last approved amount will be treated as appropriated, and the treasury may make needed payments with the governor’s advice until the legislature acts.

1090.s: This order restores certain land in Arizona to the public domain. The land had been withdrawn for use of the Papago Indians, and it includes Section 16 and sections 19 to 36 in township 5 south of range 5 west of the Gila and Salt River meridian.

1085.s: This order changes a previous order about railroad cars in the Canal Zone being equipped with safety appliances. It says the order takes effect within six months, except for old French dump cars used on the Panama Canal and the locomotive couplers needed to run them, which are covered later on July 1, 1910.

1077.s: This order changes how official communications and reports about certain U.S. territories and possessions are sent. It says these reports should go directly to the heads of the government departments as provided by law. If Congress has not named a department, the reports must be sent to the Secretary of the Interior under rules he sets.

1083.s: This order changes the schedule of United States consular fees. It sets or updates fees for extra certificates, sealing cars from Canada or Mexico, acknowledgments of deeds or powers of attorney, copies, translations, and recording unofficial documents. It also says there is no fee for certain pension-related oaths and for services done on written orders of the Department of State for official government use.

1072.s: The order lets the Civil Service Commission allow Navy yard or station employees to take part in a local election if the Secretary of the Navy thinks strict civil service rules would affect the result and the issue matters to the local welfare of government employees nearby. This can happen only after the Commission investigates as it sees fit. Employees who are given this privilege must still do their official jobs and must not cause public scandal.

1065.s: This order says unclassified laborers may be assigned to classified work only incidentally, not as their main job. It applies in departments, independent offices, and bureaus where the work cannot be done conveniently and economically by classified employees. Such assignments need the prior consent of the Civil Service Commission.

1071.s: This order creates the General Supply Committee to coordinate purchases of supplies used by more than one department or government establishment. The committee must make a general schedule of needed supplies, arrange advertisements and proposals, and submit recommendations to the Board of Awards. It also must set up a uniform method for inspecting and testing supplies, and department heads may assign employees to help when asked.

1062.s: This order directs department heads to comply with Senate or House resolutions asking for information. If a department head thinks giving the information would be incompatible with the public interest, the matter must be referred to the President for direction.

1060.s: This order changes a previous rule about admitting deaf mutes to civil service examinations. It allows them to take exams for classified civil service jobs if the heads of the Executive Departments think they can do the work. Each department must give the Civil Service Commission a list of those jobs, and the Commission will certify or withhold deaf mutes based on that list.

1061.s: The order refers a dispute over branding requirements for whisky to the Solicitor General. It says some distillers and importers asked for a hearing on an Internal Revenue order that would require some whiskies to be branded as imitations or compounds. The Solicitor General is to take testimony and report to the President on what whisky meant to manufacturers, the trade, and consumers, and whether the term covered different kinds of products.

1052.s: This order changes Civil Service Rule X about transferring an employee to another position. It says an employee may be transferred only if the Commission judges that the employee has the experience, qualifications, or training needed for the job and that transfer is needed instead of an original appointment or promotion.

1044.s: This order reserves Walrus Island and Otter Island in the Pribilof group as the Pribilof Reservation. It sets the land apart for the Department of Agriculture as a preserve and breeding ground for native birds. It makes it unlawful for anyone to hunt, trap, capture, disturb, or kill birds there, or take their eggs, unless allowed by rules from the Secretary of Agriculture.

1000.s: This order restores certain unallotted lands in New Mexico to the public domain. These lands had been set apart for use by Indians as an addition to the Navajo Reservation. It does not apply to the listed lands with 110 unapproved allotments, which are excepted from the restoration.

744.s: This order amends an earlier order that had set apart certain lands in Arizona and New Mexico as an addition to the Navajo Indian Reservation. It changes the land description so it no longer conflicts in part with an earlier order about the Jicarilla Indian Reservation in New Mexico. The order affects the boundaries of the Navajo Reservation and nearby reservation lands in Arizona and New Mexico.

743.s: This executive order changes a previous order that set apart land for the Indians of the Jicarilla Indian Reservation in New Mexico and for an addition to the Navajo Indian Reservation in New Mexico. It replaces the land description with a new boundary description for the tract of land set apart.

u-tr-19080128.s: This order amends an earlier land order for the Jicarilla Indian Reservation in New Mexico. It changes the description of the land set apart for that reservation because it partly conflicts with an earlier order adding land to the Navajo Indian Reservation. The change affects the land boundaries for the Jicarilla Indian Reservation and the related Navajo reservation addition.

711.s: This order withdraws certain lands in New Mexico from sale and settlement. It sets the land apart for Indian purposes for the use of the Indians of the Jicarilla Indian Reservation. Existing valid rights are not affected.

709.s: This order withdraws a described tract of land in Arizona and New Mexico from sale and settlement. It sets the land apart for the use of Indians as an addition to the present Navajo Reservation. It does not affect any existing valid rights of any person.
