The property is real estate, buildings, or other property that was seized or held as belonging to the late rebel government. It also covers funds from the rent, sale, or other handling of that property that have not been paid into the Treasury of the United States.

u-ajohnson-18651009.s: The order deals with land on the coast of South Carolina, Georgia, and Florida that had been set apart for refugees and freedmen. It directs Major-General Howard to go to those states and try to work out an agreement between the freedmen and the landowners. If a satisfactory agreement is reached, he is authorized to issue the needed orders after looking into the interests of both sides.

u-ajohnson-18650919.s: This order says military commanders in Georgia cannot decide disputes over contracts or property between private people, and any such actions already taken are void. It also forbids military officers from being interested in sales or contracts for cotton or other products from the state, or from using government transportation for private shipments of those products. Major-General Steedman is directed to enforce the order and report on actions by certain officers.

u-ajohnson-18650907.s: This order suspends a prior order that required Treasury officers, military officers, and other U.S. officers to turn over certain funds to the authorized officers of the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands. The funds were those collected by tax or otherwise for refugees or freedmen, or from abandoned lands or property set apart for their use.

u-ajohnson-18650916.s: This order directs the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands to provide transportation for destitute refugees and freedmen who depend on the government for support, so they can travel to places where they can find work and support themselves. It also provides free transportation for certain teachers and other people approved by the Bureau who work for refugees and freedmen. Stores and schoolbooks needed for their support and instruction may also be transported at government expense, and army officers traveling on public duty under Bureau orders may receive mileage or actual transportation costs if transport is not already provided.

u-ajohnson-18650807.s: The order says people with business with the executive government should make their requests in writing to the head of the department assigned by law. Those requests are to be considered by department heads, subject to the President’s approval. It says personal interviews with the President or heads of departments will not be granted to all visitors. It affects people who have business with the executive government.

u-ajohnson-18650825.s: Paroled prisoners who ask for passports as citizens of the United States, and against whom no special charges are pending, may get passports from the Department of State. Those passports are issued on the condition that they do not return to the United States without the President’s leave. Other people implicated in the rebellion who want to go abroad must also apply to the Department of State, and their requests will be decided case by case.

u-ajohnson-18650715.s: This order changes an earlier order about Samuel Arnold, Samuel A. Mudd, Edward Spangler, and Michael O'Laughlin. It directs that they be held at hard labor in the military prison at Dry Tortugas, Florida, for the periods set in their sentences, and that they be transported there under guard. It also dissolves the military commission led by Major-General David Hunter.

u-ajohnson-18650705.s: The order approves the sentences in the cases of eight named people. It orders that David E. Herold, George A. Atzerodt, Lewis Payne, and Mary E. Surratt be put to death by military authority on July 7, 1865. It also orders that Samuel Arnold, Samuel A. Mudd, Edward Spangler, and Michael O'Laughlin be confined at hard labor in the penitentiary at Albany, New York, for the periods set in their sentences.

u-ajohnson-18650609.s: The order says Indians in New Mexico have been seized and reduced into slavery. It directs the heads of executive departments to tell their subordinates, agents, and employees in that territory to discourage that practice and use lawful means to stop it. It affects those officials in New Mexico and the Indians mentioned in the order.

u-ajohnson-18650705-2.s: This order records the trial of several people by a military commission in Washington, D.C. It says they were charged with joining a plot to kill Abraham Lincoln and to attack or target Andrew Johnson, William H. Seward, and Ulysses S. Grant. The order also gives sentences of death to several of the accused, including David E. Herold, George A. Atzerodt, Lewis Payne, and Mary E. Surratt.

u-ajohnson-18650606.s: This order removes the prohibition on the gunboat Fusyama leaving for its destination. The Secretary of the Treasury is directed to issue a clearance for it, and the Secretary of the Navy is told not to stop it.

u-ajohnson-18650607.s: This order says people in the excepted classes named in the President's amnesty proclamation must first take and sign the oath or affirmation in that proclamation before their pardon requests will be considered. It also says anyone seeking a special pardon must apply in writing and send the original signed oath with the application.

u-ajohnson-18650606-2.s: This order directs that certain prisoners of war in the North be released after they take an oath of allegiance. It applies to enlisted men of the rebel army and petty officers and seamen of the rebel navy, and to some officers below certain ranks. Prison commanders are told to release prisoners in order, and the Quartermaster's Department will provide transportation to the nearest accessible point to their homes.

u-ajohnson-18650602.s: This order rescinds a previous rule that required passports from all travelers entering the United States, except immigrant passengers coming directly to an American port from a foreign country. It says that change does not excuse any enemies of the United States or offenders against its peace and dignity who later seek to enter the country or are found within its lawful jurisdiction.

u-ajohnson-18650602-2.s: This order directs Treasury Department officers, military officers, and other U.S. officers to turn over abandoned lands and property to authorized officers of the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands. It also requires them to transfer funds collected for refugees or freedmen, or from abandoned lands or property set apart for their use, along with related official records.

u-ajohnson-18650602-3.s: This order ends all military restrictions on trade in the states and territories of the United States. It keeps restrictions on items listed as contraband of war, including arms, ammunition, gray cloth, railroad equipment, and telegraph supplies.

u-ajohnson-18650531.s: This order closes the Executive Office and the various departments for the day on June 1. It says this is because of the assassination of Abraham Lincoln.

u-ajohnson-18650527.s: This order says that prison sentences given by military tribunals during the war are to be remitted. It also directs that the prisoners be discharged and that the Adjutant-General issue the needed instructions right away.

u-ajohnson-18650509.s: This order declares null and void the acts and proceedings of the rebel political, military, and civil organizations in Virginia and says people claiming authority under them will be treated as in rebellion against the United States. It directs federal departments to enforce United States laws in Virginia, including revenue, postal, court, naval, war, and interior matters. It also says the Federal Government will help Governor Francis H. Peirpoint take lawful steps to extend and administer the state government across Virginia.

u-ajohnson-18650509-2.s: This order changes the members of a military commission appointed in Special Orders No. 211. It relieves Cyrus B. Comstock and Horace Porter from the commission and puts James A. Ekin and C. H. Tompkins in their places. The order also lists the full membership of the commission and names Joseph Holt as judge-advocate and recorder.

u-ajohnson-18650507.s: This order appoints Hon. John A. Bingham as a special judge-advocate. He is to help the Judge-Advocate-General in the prosecution of Herold and others before the military commission presided over by Major-General Hunter.

u-ajohnson-18650506.s: This order appoints a military commission to meet in Washington, D.C., to try David E. Herold, George A. Atzerodt, Lewis Payne, Michael O'Laughlin, Edward Spangler, Samuel Arnold, Mary E. Surratt, Samuel A. Mudd, and other prisoners brought before it. It says the commission will hear charges connected to the murder of Abraham Lincoln, the attempted assassination of William H. Seward, and an alleged conspiracy to assassinate other federal officers at Washington City. The order also names the officers who will serve on the commission and says the judge-advocate will be Joseph Holt.

u-ajohnson-18650504.s: This order closes the Executive Office and the various departments at 12 noon on the day of Abraham Lincoln’s funeral in Springfield, Illinois. It applies to the Executive Office and the various departments.

u-ajohnson-18650501.s: The order directs that nine military officers be detailed to serve as a commission to try the people implicated in the murder of Abraham Lincoln, the attempted assassination of William H. Seward, and an alleged conspiracy to assassinate other federal officers in Washington City. It also directs the Judge-Advocate-General to bring charges and conduct the trials. Brevet Major-General Hartranft is assigned to help with the trial, attend the commission, and carry out its orders.

u-ajohnson-18650503.s: This order cancels two earlier rules that had blocked the export of arms and ammunition from the United States. It also ends the ban on exporting horses, mules, and live stock.

u-ajohnson-18650429-2.s: This order lifts many restrictions on internal, domestic, and coastwise trade in parts of several states under national military occupation. It still keeps restrictions required by Congress and Treasury rules, and it excludes certain war-related goods like arms, ammunition, railroad materials, and telegraph equipment. It also revokes military and naval orders that were blocking that trade and tells officers not to interfere with it under proper authority.

u-ajohnson-18650429.s: This order rescinds the earlier order that had prohibited the exportation of hay. The change takes effect on May 1, 1865, and it affects people and businesses involved in exporting hay.

u-lincoln-18650404.s: This order directs the State Department to pay a $1,000 reward for the capture of each offender who crossed the borders of the United States or entered its ports by sea and was convicted by a civil or military tribunal. It also says a $500 reward will be paid for the arrest of any person who aided and abetted those offenders in the United States. The rewards apply to people who committed capital felonies against the property or life of American citizens.

u-lincoln-18650327.s: This order directs that the United States flag be raised at Fort Sumter and saluted with guns and other salutes. It also calls for ceremonies to be held there under military direction, with a public address by the Rev. Henry Ward Beecher. Naval forces at Charleston and their commander are invited to take part.

u-lincoln-18650308.s: This order changes a previous passport rule for people entering the United States. It cancels the passport requirement for persons entering from Canada, but leaves the rest of the order in force. It affects travelers entering the country, especially those coming from Canada.

u-lincoln-18650314.s: This order says people in the United States who have traded or had contact by sea with the insurgents and who are citizens or domiciled aliens must be arrested and held as prisoners of war until the war ends. It also says they can still be prosecuted for spying or other offenses against the laws of war. Nonresident foreigners who have violated the blockade of insurgent ports must leave the United States and cannot return during the war. United States marshals and provost-marshals must arrest people who break this order, even if they have passports.

u-lincoln-18650221.s: The Department of State buildings will be lit up on the night of Washington's birthday. This is to honor the recent triumphs of the Union.

u-lincoln-18650213.s: This order asks military officers in West Tennessee to relieve people from burdens, harassments, and oppressions as far as they can while still meeting military needs. It says the goal of the war is to restore and keep peace and good government. It also tells the officers to help, not hinder, progress in that direction.

u-lincoln-18650206.s: This order sets up a board to review the quotas and credits for the states and districts under the call of December 19, 1864. If the board finds errors, it must make corrections allowed by law and facts and report its decision to the Provost-Marshal-General. The board’s decision is final, and the draft must be made to match it. The Provost-Marshal-General is also ordered to make the draft in the districts as soon as possible after the 15th of the month.

u-lincoln-18650120.s: This order directs that no clearances be granted for the export of hay from the United States until further orders. It does not apply to hay that had already been placed on shipboard before the order was published.

u-lincoln-18641231.s: This order designates several bank and railroad offices as places where the Union Pacific Railroad Company must keep books open to receive subscriptions to its capital stock. It affects the Union Pacific Railroad Company and people who want to subscribe to that stock.

u-lincoln-18641217.s: The order says that, except for immigrant passengers entering an American port by sea, no traveler may enter the United States from a foreign country without a passport. It says U.S. citizens must have a passport from the State Department or a U.S. minister or consul abroad, and aliens must have a passport from their own country that is countersigned by a U.S. diplomatic agent or consul. It says the rule is meant especially for people coming from the neighboring British Provinces and will be enforced by U.S. officers, with state and municipal authorities asked to help.

u-lincoln-18641210.s: This order appoints two special commissioners to investigate and report on the civil and military administration in the military division bordering upon and west of the Mississippi. It lets them examine witnesses under oath and gather testimony, books, papers, writings, and documents. Officers and other people in federal service must appear and testify if subpoenaed. The Secretary of War may also direct them to look into other matters and provide them with aid and compensation.

u-lincoln-18641203.s: This order says the war steamer Funayma Solace should not be allowed to go to Japan. If the Secretary of the Navy finds it fits U.S. service, he may buy it. The purchase money would be held in trust to pay any valid claims from the Japanese government about building and not delivering the steamer.

u-lincoln-18641114.s: The order accepts George B. McClellan’s resignation as a major-general in the United States Army, dated November 8, 1864. It also appoints Philip H. Sheridan as a major-general in the United States Army, with rank from November 8, 1864. This affects those two officers and their Army status.

u-lincoln-18641012.s: This order suspends, for the present, the request to clear the war vessel Fusigama so it can leave New York for Japan. It affects the Japanese Government’s vessel and its move to Japan.

u-lincoln-18641001.s: This order directs an official thank-you for volunteers from Indiana, Illinois, Iowa, and Wisconsin who served for one hundred days in the military force of the United States. It says they helped in the campaign of General Sherman and in operations in the Southwest and Georgia. The Secretary of War is directed to send the order to the four governors and to deliver certificates of honorable service to the officers and soldiers who served.

u-lincoln-18640924.s: This order lets approved agents buy products from States declared in insurrection at designated places of purchase. It allows people with the proper certificates to transport those products and some related merchandise, and it says they must be given safe conduct. It also bars military, naval, and certain civil officers from trading in these products or furnishing transportation for them, and it punishes unauthorized transport or interference with safe conduct.

u-lincoln-18640910.s: This order directs an official acknowledgment of the Ohio National Guard’s service during recent campaigns. It gives them the nation’s thanks through the governor of Ohio. The Secretary of War is directed to send the order to the governor and deliver a certificate of honorable service to the officers and soldiers who served as volunteers for one hundred days.

u-lincoln-18640903.s: The order directs a 100-gun salute at the Washington arsenal and navy-yard, and then at each arsenal and navy-yard in the United States, for recent achievements of the fleet and land forces in the harbor of Mobile and in the reduction of Fort Powell, Fort Gaines, and Fort Morgan. It also directs another 100-gun salute at several arsenals and navy-yards for the achievements of the army under Major-General Sherman in Georgia and the capture of Atlanta. The Secretary of War and the Secretary of the Navy are to issue the directions needed to carry it out.

u-lincoln-18640903-3.s: The President gives the nation’s thanks to Major-General William T. Sherman and the officers and soldiers under his command before Atlanta. It says their campaign in Georgia led to the capture of Atlanta and included marches, battles, sieges, and other military operations.

u-lincoln-18640831.s: This order says that people bringing out cotton under authority from the Secretary of the Treasury must not be stopped by the War Department, the Navy Department, or any other government department. It applies to anyone involved in bringing out cotton under that authority.

u-lincoln-18640903-2.s: The President gives the nation’s thanks to Admiral Farragut and Major-General Canby for planning and carrying out the recent operations in Mobile Harbor and against Fort Powell, Fort Gaines, and Fort Morgan. It also thanks Admiral Farragut, Major-General Granger, the commanders on sea and land, and the sailors and soldiers who took part for their energy and courage.

u-lincoln-18640718.s: This order says the executive government will receive and consider any proposal for peace that also keeps the Union together and ends slavery. It says the person carrying such a proposal will be given safe conduct both ways.

u-lincoln-18640518.s: This order directs the arrest and imprisonment of the editors, proprietors, and publishers of the New York World and the New York Journal of Commerce. It also orders the military to take over their printing plants, stop any further publication from them, and hold the arrested people for trial before a military commission. It also applies to anyone who prints the same publication after notice that it was false.

u-lincoln-18640509.s: The order recommends that patriots give thanks and pray to Almighty God. It asks people to do this at home, in places of public worship, and wherever they may be.

u-lincoln-18640423.s: The President accepts a plan from the governors of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Iowa, and Wisconsin to provide infantry troops for the approaching campaign. The troops are to serve for 100 days, be mustered into United States service, and be used in fortifications or wherever needed, within or outside their states. They are to be clothed, armed, equipped, subsisted, transported, and paid like other United States infantry volunteers, with no bounty paid and no charge or credit on any draft. The Secretary of War is directed to carry the plan into effect.

u-lincoln-18640416.s: The order withholds certain townships from sale for the proposed enlargement of the Little Traverse Reservation. It says this would make room to move Indians from Mackinac, Beaver Island, Thunder Bay, and areas east of Grand Traverse Bay to that reservation.

u-lincoln-18640402.s: This order extends a previous export rule to prohibit exporting all classes of salted provisions from any part of the United States to any foreign port. It allows meats cured, salted, or packed in a State or Territory bordering on the Pacific Ocean to be exported from any port in that State or Territory.

u-lincoln-18640314.s: This order calls for 200,000 men for military service in the Army, Navy, and Marine Corps of the United States. It sets quotas for wards, towns, townships, precincts, election districts, and counties, with credits and deficiencies from earlier quotas taken into account. Men could be raised by voluntary enlistment until April 15, 1864, and drafts would begin after that if quotas were not filled. It also says government bounties continue until April 1, 1864, after which only a $100 bounty would be paid.

u-lincoln-18640312.s: This order relieves Major-General H. W. Halleck from duty as General in Chief of the Army at his own request. It assigns Lieutenant-General U. S. Grant to command the armies of the United States, and says the Army headquarters will be in Washington and with Grant in the field. It also assigns Major-General W. T. Sherman to the Military Division of the Mississippi and Major-General J. B. McPherson to the Department and Army of the Tennessee.

u-lincoln-18640310.s: This order assigns Lieutenant-General Ulysses S. Grant to command the armies of the United States. It affects the United States Army and gives Grant that military command.

u-lincoln-18640307.s: This order sets the starting point for the Union Pacific Railroad Company’s railroad and telegraph line on the western boundary of Iowa. It places that point east of and opposite the east line of section 10 in township 15 north, range 13 east, of the sixth principal meridian in the Territory of Nebraska. The order applies to the company named in the act of Congress about building the railroad and telegraph line to the Pacific Ocean.

u-lincoln-18640307-2.s: This order directs that certain tobacco belonging to the French Government may be exported from insurgent territory. The export is limited to no more than 7,000 hogsheads, and it must be the same tobacco the French Government first asked to export.

u-lincoln-18640226.s: This order changes the punishment for deserters who had been sentenced to death by court-martial and had not already been acted on by the President. Their sentences are to be reduced to imprisonment during the war at Dry Tortugas, Florida, and they are to be sent there under guard. In special cases, commanding generals may restore deserters under sentence to duty if they think the service will benefit.

u-lincoln-18640201.s: This order directs a draft for 500,000 men for military service in the United States. The men are to serve for three years or during the war, and credit is to be given for men already enlisted or drafted before March 1 and not already counted.

u-lincoln-18640201-2.s: The order directs the War Department to send a transport to the United States colony at the island of Vache in San Domingo to bring back colonists who want to return. Those who come back are to be taken to Washington unless told otherwise, and they are to be employed and provided for at camps for colored persons around that city. Only colonists who choose to return, and their belongings, are to be brought back.

u-lincoln-18640126.s: This order approves additional trade regulations set by the Secretary of the Treasury. It says that property brought in for sale in good faith, and actually sold under certain listed regulations after they take effect, will not be confiscated or forfeited to the United States. It affects people bringing in property for sale under those regulations.

u-lincoln-18640115.s: The order approved reserving a tract of land in New Mexico, 40 miles square with Bosque Redondo as the center, for the Apache Indians. It says the land should be withheld from pre-emption and settlement and set apart for Indian purposes. This affects the Apache Indians and anyone seeking to settle or claim that land.

u-lincoln-18640112.s: The order says that orders and records about the Missouri State Militia and the Enrolled Missouri Militia kept in Missouri headquarters offices must be open to inspection by the Missouri general assembly or people it sends. It also says copies of those records must be given to them when requested.

u-lincoln-18631221.s: This order publishes a joint resolution thanking Major-General Ulysses S. Grant and the officers and soldiers who fought under his command during the rebellion. It requests the President to have a gold medal made for Grant, along with a parchment copy of the resolution to be sent to him. It also sets aside money to carry out the resolution.

u-lincoln-18640109.s: This order says Caleb B. Smith, former Secretary of the Interior, has died at his home in Indiana. It directs the executive buildings at the seat of Government to be draped in mourning, and the Secretary of State to send a copy of the order to his family with the President’s and department heads’ sympathy.

u-lincoln-18631207.s: The order says the insurgent force is retreating from east Tennessee, and it says this may leave Union forces in that position. It recommends that all loyal people gather at their places of worship and give special homage and gratitude to Almighty God for this advancement of the national cause.

u-lincoln-18631110.s: This order allows certain tobacco in the United States that belongs to the governments of France, Austria, or any other state at peace with the United States to be exported from U.S. ports. The tobacco must have been bought and paid for before March 4, 1861. The export must happen under the supervision and responsibility of those governments' naval officers and follow regulations set by the Secretary of State.

u-lincoln-18630924.s: This order authorizes Major-General Hooker to take military possession of railroads, along with their cars, locomotives, plants, and equipment, if needed for the military operation under his charge. It directs officers, agents, and employees of those railroads to help him and obey his commands.

u-lincoln-18630904.s: This order changes an earlier export ban. It allows arms that were already imported into the United States to be sent back to their original place of shipment. It also allows live stock raised in any state or territory on the Pacific Ocean to be exported from ports in that state or territory.

u-lincoln-18630831.s: This order changes an earlier rule that banned exporting arms, ammunition, and munitions of war from the United States. It allows imported arms, ammunition, and munitions of war to be sent back to the ports they were shipped from for the United States.

u-lincoln-18630825.s: This order lets vessels or merchandise bound for New Orleans enter the port if they have Treasury Department clearances for military needs and are certified by the military governor of Louisiana. It also lets vessels and domestic produce from New Orleans move to another port if the military governor permits it and the destination port is not blockaded by the United States.

u-lincoln-18630730.s: This order says the United States will give the same protection to all its soldiers, no matter their color. It says if the enemy kills a U.S. soldier in violation of the laws of war, a rebel soldier will be executed. If the enemy enslaves or sells a U.S. soldier into slavery because of color, a rebel soldier in U.S. custody will be put to hard labor until that prisoner is released and treated as a prisoner of war.

u-lincoln-18630709.s: This order revokes the appointment of John S. Phelps as military governor of Arkansas and Amos F. Eno as secretary. It also abolishes the office of military governor in Arkansas. All authority, appointments, and power given to them or to anyone acting under them is revoked and annulled.

u-lincoln-18630725.s: The order directs the Secretary of the Navy to add instructions for naval commanders about contraband trade. It says they should avoid using neutral ports to watch neutral vessels and then seize them when they leave. It also says they must not hold the crew of a captured neutral vessel, or other subjects of a neutral power, as prisoners of war except for a small number needed as witnesses in prize court.

u-lincoln-18630622.s: This order assigns Associate Justice Stephen J. Field to the tenth circuit. It affects the Supreme Court justice and the circuit courts of California and Oregon.

u-lincoln-18630704.s: The President announces news from the Army of the Potomac and says it reflects great honor on that army and the Union cause. He also asks that people remember God on this day and feel sympathy for the many fallen.

u-lincoln-18630331.s: This order licenses and permits commercial intercourse between citizens of loyal States and the inhabitants of insurrectionary States. It applies only in the cases and under the restrictions set out in regulations from the Secretary of the Treasury, with the President's approval. It affects people in those States who trade with each other.

u-lincoln-18630125.s: This order relieves Major-General A. E. Burnside from command of the Army of the Potomac at his own request. It also relieves Major-General E. V. Sumner and Major-General W. B. Franklin from duty in the Army of the Potomac, and assigns Major-General J. Hooker to command it. The officers relieved are to report in person to the army’s adjutant-general.

u-lincoln-18630121.s: This order sets the uniform width of the track for the railroad and all of its branches at 5 feet. It applies to the railroad built under the act of Congress and to the company that asked to fix the gauge for a branch line.

u-lincoln-18630108.s: The order gives the Attorney-General control over proceedings under a 1861 law that confiscates property used for insurrectionary purposes. It extends that same supervision to court cases about the property of rebels and traitors under that law, as well as under the 1862 law named in the order.

u-lincoln-18630104.s: This order asks the Secretary of the Navy to consider requests from people who are loyal to the Union and are refugees from rebel oppression in Virginia. It lets the Navy help these people move their families and property to protection within Union lines by armed gunboats on the Potomac River and Chesapeake Bay, if the help fits naval efficiency and military expediency.

u-lincoln-18621222.s: This message thanks the officers and soldiers of the Army of the Potomac for their service after the battle of Fredericksburg. It says the attempt was not an error, praises their courage and skill, and notes that they crossed and recrossed the river in front of the enemy. It also offers sympathy for those who were killed or badly wounded.

u-lincoln-18621121.s: This order stops arms, ammunition, and other munitions of war from being cleared for export from the United States until further order. It also cancels earlier export clearances that had not yet left the country and directs the Secretary of War to keep possession of arms recently seized at Rouses Point that were bound for Canada.

u-lincoln-18621115.s: This order directs officers and men in the Army and Navy to observe the Sabbath. It says Sunday labor should be reduced to strict necessity. It also says military discipline and the cause they defend should not be harmed by disrespect for the day.

u-lincoln-18621113.s: The order puts the Attorney General in charge of proceedings under the act of Congress about seizing and confiscating the property of rebels and traitors. It also lets the Attorney General give instructions to U.S. attorneys and marshals about these seizures, prosecutions, and condemnations. If there is reason to fear resistance, those officers may call on military officers for help, protection, and support, and commanding officers must obey that call when they can.

u-lincoln-18621112.s: This order allows Treasury clearances for vessels or merchandise bound for Norfolk when they are certified by the military commandant at Fort Monroe for the military needs of the department. It also lets vessels and domestic produce from Norfolk pass to another port if the military commandant at Fort Monroe permits it for the military purposes of his command, as long as the destination port is not blockaded by the United States.

u-lincoln-18621107.s: This order directs Brigadier-General Ellet to report to Rear-Admiral Porter for instructions. It says Ellet is to act under Porter's direction until the War Department orders otherwise.

u-lincoln-18621105.s: This order relieves Major-General McClellan from command of the Army of the Potomac and gives that command to Major-General Burnside. It also changes command of two corps in that army, giving one to Major-General Hunter and the other to Major-General Hooker. The General in Chief is authorized to issue the order right away or when he thinks it is proper.

u-lincoln-18621029.s: This order assigns the justices of the Supreme Court to the federal circuits then existing by law. It applies to the Supreme Court justices named in the order and sets each one to a specific circuit.

u-lincoln-18621020.s: This order creates a provisional court for Louisiana and appoints a provisional judge to run it. The judge may hear and decide civil and criminal cases, including law, equity, revenue, and admiralty cases, and may appoint a prosecuting attorney, marshal, and clerk. The appointments last at the President's pleasure and do not go beyond military occupation of New Orleans or the return of civil authority there and in Louisiana.

u-lincoln-18620903.s: This order directs Major-General Halleck to begin organizing an army for active operations as soon as possible. It says he should use all available forces under his control, but keep the forces needed for the defense of Washington separate from that active army.

u-lincoln-18620902.s: This order directs that all clerks and employees of the civil departments in Washington, along with employees on the public buildings there, be organized into companies. They are to be armed and given ammunition for the defense of the capital.

u-lincoln-18620814.s: The order changes when bounty and advanced pay will be paid to volunteers for new regiments, regiments already in the field, and regiments that are still being organized. It also says incomplete new regiments will be consolidated and extra officers mustered out if they are not filled in time. The order sets a draft for 300,000 militia and says a special draft will be ordered if the old regiments are not filled by volunteers. It also says officers now in the field must stay with their commands and will not be detailed to take new commands.

u-lincoln-18620808.s: This order says that until further notice, any citizen liable to be drafted into the militia may not leave for a foreign country. It directs U.S. marshals, military officers, and police authorities to stop and detain people who try to leave in violation of the order. It also says that anyone liable to draft who leaves their county or state before the draft can be arrested, taken to a military post, and put on military duty for the draft term. The writ of habeas corpus is suspended for people arrested and detained under this order and for people arrested for disloyal practices.

u-lincoln-18620804.s: The order calls 300,000 militia into service of the United States for nine months, unless they are discharged sooner. The Secretary of War will assign each state’s quota and set rules for the draft. If a state does not provide its quota of the additional 300,000 volunteers by August 15, the shortfall will be filled by a special draft from the militia. The War Department will also prepare rules for promoting officers for meritorious and distinguished service and for removing incompetent officers.

u-lincoln-18620731.s: This order revokes all leaves and furloughs not given by the War Department and requires all officers and privates fit for service to return to their commands. It says that after August 11, only War Department leave, wounds, or disease that makes a person unfit for duty will excuse an absence. It also orders a muster of each regiment and corps, stops pay for those absent without cause, and allows local officials to arrest and deliver absent soldiers fit for duty.

u-lincoln-18620725.s: This order announces the death of former President Martin Van Buren. It directs the Executive Mansion and all Executive Departments except War and Navy to be placed in mourning and says business will be suspended for one day. It also directs the War and Navy Departments to pay military and naval honors, and it orders troops, the flag, gun salutes, and mourning dress for Army officers and regimental colors.

u-lincoln-18620722.s: Military commanders in Virginia, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, and Arkansas are ordered to seize and use property needed for military purposes. They are also ordered to employ people of African descent as laborers for military or naval purposes and give them reasonable wages. Records must be kept on the property and the people used, so compensation can be made in proper cases.

u-lincoln-18620721.s: This order says aliens living in the United States must obey the laws and respect the government. It says they cannot be required to take an oath of allegiance to the United States, and any such oaths already taken are canceled. Military commanders are told not to require those oaths in the future, and to report any orders that affect an alien's personal liberty.

u-lincoln-18620711.s: This order directs that the Southwest Branch of the Pacific Railroad in Missouri be repaired, extended, and completed from Rolla to Lebanon, toward Springfield. It says the work is to make the line available for the Government’s military use. The Secretary of War is directed to carry out the order and may take possession and control of the railroad line and related property if needed.

u-lincoln-18620711-2.s: The order assigns Major-General Henry W. Halleck to command the whole land forces of the United States as General in Chief. It also directs him to go to the capital as soon as he can safely do so without hurting the positions and operations in his department.

u-lincoln-18620701.s: The order calls for an additional force of 300,000 men to be brought into service. It says the troops should be chiefly infantry. The War Department is to issue an order setting each state’s quota, so it affects the states and the men who may be enrolled.

u-lincoln-18620630.s: The order asks the governors of the states to provide 150,000 men, including men already called for by the Secretary of War. It says more troops are needed because the Army has been reduced by sickness and casualties and because national forces must hold captured places and keep a force in front of Washington. The order says the additional men are needed to take Richmond and help end the rebellion in several Southern states.

u-lincoln-18620626.s: This order combines the forces under Fremont, Banks, McDowell, and the troops under Sturgis at Washington into one army called the Army of Virginia. Major-General John Pope is put in command, and the army is divided into three corps under Fremont, Banks, and McDowell. The army is directed to protect western Virginia and the national capital, attack the forces under Jackson and Ewell, move toward Charlottesville, and help relieve General McClellan and capture Richmond.

u-lincoln-18620530.s: This order says militia regiments and three-month volunteer regiments that are ready to report at St. Louis, Columbus, or Washington City by June 10 will be mustered into the service of the United States for three months. Their pay starts from the date of enlistment. It also says 50,000 men will be accepted under the call for three-years' volunteers as raised and reported by the state governors.

u-lincoln-18620525.s: This order takes military possession of all railroads in the United States until further order. It requires railroad companies, officers, and workers to be ready to carry troops and war supplies when ordered by military authorities, and to stop other business while doing so.

u-lincoln-18620528.s: This order appoints Colonel Haupt as chief of construction and transportation in the Department of the Rappahannock, with the rank of colonel, and puts him on Major-General McDowell’s staff. It authorizes him to open military railroads for use, use them for transportation, hire assistants and employees, and use government steamers and transports. It also lets him take possession of and use railroads, engines, cars, buildings, machinery, and related equipment within the department.

u-lincoln-18620405.s: The order gives Major-General John A. Dix authority over the police in Baltimore. It lets him remove the civil police, set up a military police, arrest and imprison disloyal persons, declare martial law, and suspend habeas corpus in Baltimore or part of his command. It also directs that thanks be given to Major-General John E. Wool and the officers and soldiers under his command for their actions at Norfolk and nearby places.

u-lincoln-18620315.s: This order thanks Lieutenant John L. Worden and the crew of the Monitor for their actions in the naval fight with the Merrimac at Hampton Roads. It says the Monitor engaged a stronger armored ship, repelled it after a few hours, and that Worden was injured. It also says a copy of the letter will be read to the officers and crew of the Monitor.

u-lincoln-18620313.s: This order tells Major-General George B. McClellan how to carry out the army’s plan. It says to leave enough force at Manassas Junction so the enemy cannot take it back, keep Washington entirely secure, and move the rest of the army down the Potomac to a new base or at once in pursuit of the enemy.

u-lincoln-18620311.s: This order changes command of several military departments. Major-General McClellan keeps command of the Department of the Potomac, and Major-General Halleck is placed in command of the new Department of the Mississippi. It also creates the Mountain Department, to be commanded by Major-General Fremont, and tells department commanders to report directly to the Secretary of War.

u-lincoln-18620308.s: This order reorganizes part of the Army of the Potomac into four army corps and names the officers who will command each one. It also says the forces left to defend Washington will be placed under Brigadier-General James S. Wadsworth, who will also be military governor of the District of Columbia. A fifth army corps will be formed under Major-General N. P. Banks from his own division and General Shields’s division.

u-lincoln-18620308-2.s: This order limits how much of the Army of the Potomac can be moved before Washington is kept secure and the Potomac route to the Chesapeake Bay is cleared, unless the President gives permission. It also directs the Army and Navy to work together to capture enemy batteries on the Potomac between Washington and the Chesapeake Bay. The order affects the Army of the Potomac, the General in Chief, and the Army and Navy.

u-lincoln-18620228.s: This order allows some trade between people in areas that had been declared in insurrection and people in the loyal states of the Union. That trade must follow rules set or approved by the Secretary of the Treasury. It applies to commercial intercourse on the inland waters and ways of the United States.

u-lincoln-18620227.s: This order appoints a special commission to examine the cases of state prisoners held in military custody by the United States. The commissioners must decide whether each prisoner should be released, kept in military custody, or sent to civil courts for trial. They are also directed to hear the cases in a summary way and report their findings to the War Department.

u-lincoln-18620225.s: The President takes military possession of all telegraph lines in the United States. It forbids telegraphic messages about military operations unless authorized by the War Department or military commanders. Newspapers that publish unauthorized military news will be barred from getting information by telegraph or sending papers by railroad. The order says this control is not meant to interfere with the normal business of the companies or private business.

u-lincoln-18620218.s: The President tells Brigadier-General F. W. Lander that he has noticed the activity and enterprise shown by Lander and the officers and soldiers under his command. It says their success shows what can be done in bad weather and on bad roads by a small force that stays ready to face the enemy.

u-lincoln-18620218-2.s: The President gives thanks to Brigadier-General Burnside, Flag-Officer Goldsborough, Brigadier-General Grant, Flag-Officer Foote, and the land and naval forces under them for the capture of Fort Henry and Roanoke Island. He says he will honor the living for their bravery and pay fitting honor to the memory of the dead.

u-lincoln-18620218-3.s: This order publishes Congress’s resolutions about reading George Washington’s Farewell Address. It directs that selected parts of the address be read to the Army and Navy on February 22. It also orders the address, or parts of it, to be read to troops at every military post and at the head of Army regiments and corps.

u-lincoln-18620218-4.s: This order directs that captured rebel flags be presented to Congress in the Hall of the House of Representatives after George Washington’s Farewell Address is read. Congress would then decide how to dispose of the flags.

u-lincoln-18620213.s: This order says that all requests to go south across the military lines of the United States must be sent to Major-General John A. Dix in Baltimore. He may grant or refuse them, and prisoners of war or other released prisoners must report to him when they arrive in Baltimore and follow his directions. It also ends the old rule that passes across the military lines had to be signed by the Secretary of State and countersigned by the general commanding.

u-lincoln-18620214.s: This order directs that political prisoners and state prisoners held in military custody be released if they sign a parole promising not to aid the enemies of the United States. It says the Secretary of War may except spies and others whose release would not be safe. It also grants amnesty for past treason or disloyalty to people who are released and keep their parole. Future extraordinary arrests are to be made only under military authority.

u-lincoln-18620211.s: This order appoints D.C. McCallum as military director and superintendent of railroads in the United States. It gives him authority to take possession of and use railroads, engines, cars, locomotives, and related equipment. The purpose is to move troops, arms, ammunition, and other military supplies safely and quickly.

u-lincoln-18620131.s: It directs the disposable force of the Army of the Potomac, after safely defending Washington, to form an expedition for a military move. The goal is to seize and occupy a point on the railroad southwest of Manassas Junction. The General in Chief is given the details, and the expedition is to move before or on February 22.

u-lincoln-18620127.s: This order sets February 22, 1862 as the day for a general movement of the United States land and naval forces against the insurgent forces. It names forces at Fortress Monroe, the Army of the Potomac, the Army of Western Virginia, the army near Munfordville, the army and flotilla at Cairo, and a naval force in the Gulf of Mexico as needing to be ready to move. It also requires all other land and naval forces to follow existing orders and be ready for additional orders, and it holds department heads and commanders responsible for prompt execution.

u-lincoln-18620122.s: The order says United States forces won a victory over armed traitors and rebels at Mill Springs, Kentucky. It thanks the officers and soldiers who won the battle and says their courage will be recognized and rewarded when official reports are received. It also says the Army is expected to show courage, daring, and patriotic zeal against the rebellious enemy.

u-lincoln-18611230.s: This order directs that a joint resolution be read at the head of every regiment in the Army of the United States. The resolution gives Congress’s recognition and thanks to the late Brigadier-General Nathaniel Lyon and the officers and soldiers under his command for their service at the battle of Springfield, Missouri. It also authorizes each regiment engaged to bear the word "Springfield" on its colors in gold letters.

u-lincoln-18611202.s: This order authorizes General H. W. Halleck to suspend the writ of habeas corpus within the military division under his command in Missouri. It also lets him use martial law when he decides it is needed to protect public safety and the authority of the United States.

u-lincoln-18611127.s: This order closes the several government departments for the day of thanksgiving appointed by the municipal authorities of Washington and Georgetown. It applies to officers of the Government so they may take part in the ceremonies.

u-lincoln-18611116.s: This order says that in parts of Virginia occupied by United States forces, people may not try to exercise state, county, or municipal civil office powers under the authority of the Commonwealth of Virginia unless they are acting under the Wheeling convention and its acts. Anyone who does so is to be treated as acting hostilely against the United States and taken into military custody. Commanding officers are told to enforce the order in their own commands.

u-lincoln-18611107.s: The order lets the governor of Missouri raise a force of state militia to serve during the war. This force is to work with United States troops in Missouri, and it is not to be sent outside the state except for its immediate defense. The troops are to be armed, equipped, fed, transported, and paid by the United States while in active service, and the governor may appoint certain officers for the force.

u-lincoln-18611105.s: The order approves a plan for Missouri to raise a state militia to work with United States troops inside the state. The militia would be drilled and governed under Army rules and the Articles of War, and the United States would provide its arms, equipment, transportation, and pay while it is in service. It also accepts a change saying the governor will appoint the same person as major-general of militia who is in command of the United States Department of the West, and revoke that commission if that commander is replaced.

u-lincoln-18611101.s: Winfield Scott is placed on the retired list of the Army at his own request, and his current pay, subsistence, and allowances are not reduced. George B. McClellan is directed to take command of the Army of the United States. The Army headquarters will be in Washington, and communications to the commanding general must go through the Adjutant-General.

u-lincoln-18611014.s: The order says the military line of the United States for suppressing the insurrection may be extended as far as Bangor, Maine. It authorizes Lieutenant-General Winfield Scott and any officer acting under his authority to suspend the writ of habeas corpus in any place between Bangor and Washington, D.C.

u-lincoln-18611004.s: This order directs that certain flag-officers of the United States Navy, those authorized to wear a square flag at the mizzenmast head, will take rank with major-generals of the United States Army. It affects those Navy officers and sets their place in rank relative to Army major-generals.

u-lincoln-18611003.s: This order establishes the Uintah Valley in Utah Territory as an Indian reservation. It sets apart the entire valley of the Uintah River, extending to the first range of mountains on each side, for the use and occupancy of Indian tribes. It also reserves that land to the United States.

u-lincoln-18610807.s: This order prohibits correspondence or communication that gives the enemy information about Army operations, military movements, troops, camps, arsenals, intrenchments, or other military affairs. It applies to spoken, written, printed, and telegraphed communication without the authority and sanction of the major-general in command. People who violate it will be proceeded against under the fifty-seventh article of war.

u-lincoln-18610731.s: The order directs U.S. marshals near forts holding political prisoners to provide decent lodging and food for those prisoners. Prisoners may arrange for those things themselves if they prefer, and commanding officers must allow it.

u-lincoln-18610702.s: This order authorizes the commanding general of the Army of the United States to suspend the writ of habeas corpus when resistance is found on or near military lines between New York City and Washington. It applies where the general or the officer in command thinks suspension is necessary for public safety during the suppression of an insurrection against the laws of the United States.

u-lincoln-18610620.s: This order directs that the writ of habeas corpus may be suspended, at the officer’s discretion, for Major Chase of the Engineer Corps. It applies to Major Chase, who is described as being alleged to be guilty of treasonable practices against the government.

u-lincoln-18610507.s: This order authorizes Colonel Robert Anderson to receive volunteer troops into the Army of the United States from Kentucky and the western part of Virginia. The troops must be willing to serve for three years under the terms of the May 3, 1861 proclamation and the May 4, 1861 War Department orders. Their officers are to be commissioned by the United States.

u-lincoln-18610430.s: The President directs Army officers, except those who entered service since the 1st instant, to take the oath of allegiance to the United States again. Commanding officers must carry out the order promptly and report back.

u-lincoln-18610427.s: This order says the commanding general is suppressing an insurrection against the laws of the United States. It authorizes him, or the officer in command at the place where resistance occurs, to suspend the writ of habeas corpus for public safety on or near the military line between Philadelphia and Washington if resistance makes that necessary.

u-lincoln-18610425.s: The order says the Maryland legislature has a legal right to meet, and it should not be arrested or dispersed before it acts. It tells the Commanding General to watch what the legislature does. If it takes action to arm people against the United States, he is to use prompt and efficient means to counteract it, including, if needed, bombardment of cities and suspension of the writ of habeas corpus.

u-buchanan-18590308.s: This order announces the death of Aaron V. Brown, the Postmaster-General of the United States. It directs the Army and Navy to show mourning by firing guns, lowering flags, and wearing mourning badges or crape. It also closes the War Department and the Navy Department until after the funeral observances.

u-pierce-18530420.s: This order announces the death of Vice-President William R. King and directs mourning for him. It suspends work in the various departments, closes the public offices for one day, and orders military and naval honors. The Army, Navy, and Marine Corps are told to hold ceremonies, fly flags at half-staff or half-mast, and wear mourning badges or crape for a set time.

u-pierce-18530323.s: This order transfers control of the work on the wings of the United States Capitol from the Department of the Interior to the War Department. It also asks the Secretary of War to name a suitable officer to take charge of the work.

u-fillmore-18521025.s: This order announces the death of the Secretary of State, Daniel Webster, to the executive departments. It asks Cabinet members to wear mourning badges for thirty days and directs the Acting Secretary of State to tell foreign governments and the diplomatic corps. It affects the executive departments, the Cabinet, and U.S. diplomatic contacts abroad.

u-fillmore-18520913.s: The order asks for the necessary surveys, projects, and estimates to find the best way to provide the cities of Washington and Georgetown with a steady supply of good and wholesome water. It affects the cities of Washington and Georgetown and the work needed to plan that water supply.

u-fillmore-18520629.s: This order asks the heads of the Executive Departments to close their departments for the rest of the day. It was issued after the death of the Hon. Henry Clay. It affects the Executive Departments and the people who work there.

u-fillmore-18520517.s: It gives Hugh Maxwell, the collector at New York, authority to arrest any unlawful expedition that may be fitted out in his district. It also lets him call on military and naval officers there for help. The Secretary of War is asked to issue the needed instructions to the proper military officer in that district.

u-fillmore-18511231.s: This order reduces the reservation at the entrance of San Francisco Harbor in California. It keeps only two tracts of land: the promontory of Point Jose and the Presidio tract and Fort Point. It changes the earlier reservation that had included Fort Point, Point Jose, and the Presidio.

u-fillmore-18501106.s: This order exempts and reserves certain lands in California from sale for public purposes. It covers several tracts in the Bay of San Francisco and nearby areas, including Yerba Buena Island, Alcatrazes Island, Angel Island, Mare Island, and other listed shore lands.

u-fillmore-18500710.s: This order closes the Executive Departments until after the President’s funeral. It also places the Executive Mansion and the departments in mourning, and requires government officers to wear the usual badge of mourning for six months.

u-taylor-18490619.s: The order announces the death of James K. Polk and directs the Army and War and Navy Departments to honor his memory. It places the Executive Mansion and departments in mourning, suspends business for one day, and orders military and naval honors. It also tells military posts to parade troops, read the order, fly the flag at half-staff, fire guns, and wear mourning for six months.

u-polk-18481226.s: The Secretary of War is directed to arrange for flags, standards, and colors taken by the Army of the United States from their enemies in the recent war with Mexico to be deposited at the Military Academy at West Point. This is done under an 1814 law that says such captured items should be preserved and displayed in a public place chosen by the President.

u-polk-18480224.s: This order announces the death of John Quincy Adams to the Army and says he died while serving in the House of Representatives. It directs that executive offices in Washington be placed in mourning and that business be suspended for that day and the next. It also orders funeral honors at military stations, including a parade of troops, the flag at half-staff, gun salutes, and mourning on Army officers and regimental colors.

u-polk-18470323.s: This order says that ports and places in Mexico held by U.S. forces during the war should be opened to trade with neutral nations and the United States for non-contraband goods, if prescribed duties are paid. It directs the Treasury Department to examine Mexican duties and propose a schedule of duties and collection rules for those ports. It also says the duties will be collected by military and naval commanders and that the money will help pay war expenses.

u-polk-18450616.s: This order directs several executive departments and the Executive Mansion to be put into mourning and closed for one day. It also tells the Army, Navy, and Marine Corps to wear mourning and follow other honors for Andrew Jackson. Naval stations, public vessels, and military stations are ordered to fly flags at half-mast or half-staff and fire guns as part of the mourning.

u-tyler-18410705.s: The order directs Brevet Major-General Winfield Scott to take command as Major-General of the Army of the United States. It applies to him in his new Army role and tells him to begin his duties.

u-vanburen-18400331.s: This order sets a uniform work-hour rule for people working on public works under the President and the departments. It requires laborers and mechanics to work only the number of hours set by the ten-hour system.

u-tyler-18440229.s: The order tells U.S. diplomatic and consular officers, and other State Department officers, to wear the usual badge of mourning for thirty days after receiving it. It says this is in memory of Mr. Upshur, who died in the Princeton explosion, which also killed and wounded other people. Separate orders tell the Army and Navy to mark the deaths with mourning, half-staff flags, and gun salutes.

u-vanburen-18370307.s: The order directs the Surgeon-General of the Army to accompany former President Andrew Jackson to Wheeling, Virginia, as his medical attendant. It also directs Assistant Surgeon Reynolds to join him at Wheeling and, if ordered, continue with him to his home in Tennessee. After these duties are finished, the officers are to return to their regular stations.

u-jackson-18370218.s: This order sends back the court of inquiry’s proceedings about the failure of Major-General Scott’s campaign against the Seminole Indians in 1836. It says the court must review the evidence again and report the facts more clearly and precisely, including times, places, troop strength, and other important details. The Secretary of War is directed to send the proceedings and this order to Major-General Alexander Macomb, the court’s president, for action.

u-jackson-18370215.s: This order sends the court of inquiry’s proceedings and evidence back to the court for more action. The President disapproves the court’s opinion and tells it to review the evidence again and report the facts more clearly about the campaign against the Creek Indians. It also says the court should stay within the subjects it was ordered to examine.

u-jackson-18360807.s: The order says the requested troops from Tennessee, Kentucky, Mississippi, and Louisiana should not be called up for now. It says the volunteers already authorized by Congress were meant to be used in a set way, mainly for the Indian war in the South and to protect the western frontier. It also says some volunteers were mustered into service in excess of what was called for, and the governors of Kentucky, Mississippi, and Louisiana should withhold their quotas until further orders.

u-jackson-18310806.s: The order directs the Acting Secretary of War to report to the President for dismissal every clerk in that office who uses the insolvent debtors act for debts contracted during Andrew Jackson’s Administration. The same order was also sent to the Secretary of the Navy, so it affected clerks in both offices.

u-jackson-18340621.s: This order announces the death of General Lafayette to the Army and Navy. It directs that the same honors be paid to his memory at military and naval stations as were paid when Washington died. The order calls for guns to be fired, flags to be at half-mast, and Army officers to wear crape on the left arm for six months.

u-jackson-18290408.s: This order says no pension payments for an invalid’s disability can start until proof is filed in the Department and the Secretary decides on it. It also says no pension will be allowed to anyone while serving as an officer of the Army, except in cases already decided before.

u-jackson-18300612.s: The order says a free and full pardon is given to people who were deserters as of that date. Those under arrest for desertion are to be released and return to duty. Those who are at large or under sentence of death are discharged and cannot enter the Army or be enlisted again.

u-jqadams-18280228.s: This order announces the death of Major-General Brown to the Army. It directs Army officers to wear mourning badges for six months, and it orders guns to be fired at military posts and the National flag to be kept at half-mast on the day after the order arrives.

u-jqadams-18260711.s: This order tells the Army to honor Thomas Jefferson and John Adams after their deaths. It directs funeral honors at military stations, asks Army officers to wear mourning on the left arm, and says the Army should wear a badge of mourning. It also says the Tuesday after the order reaches each military station will be a day of rest, the national flag will fly at half-mast, and guns and cannon will be fired at set times.

u-washington-17910122.s: This order appoints Thomas Johnson, Daniel Carroll, and David Stuart as commissioners. They are to survey the district accepted for the permanent seat of the Government of the United States and do other jobs directed by law. Their authority lasts during the President’s pleasure.

12872.s: This order blocks property and interests in property of people who helped obstruct the implementation of United Nations Security Council Resolutions 841 and 873, the Governors Island Agreement, or the activities of the United Nations Mission in Haiti. It also blocks property of people who contributed to violence in Haiti or gave material or financial support to those actions. Transactions under U.S. jurisdiction that try to evade these restrictions are prohibited.

12865.s: This order declares a national emergency over UNITA’s actions in Angola. It prohibits U.S. persons from selling or supplying arms, military equipment, ammunition, and petroleum products to UNITA or to Angola outside designated points of entry. It also bars U.S. persons from transactions that evade these restrictions and directs federal agencies to carry out the order.

12852.s: This order establishes the President’s Council on Sustainable Development. The Council advises the President on sustainable development and is to recommend a national sustainable development action strategy. It is made up of up to 25 members from the public and private sectors, and executive agencies must provide information to it as needed. The order also revokes Executive Order No. 12737 and says the Council will exist for 2 years unless its charter is extended.

12853.s: This order blocks property and interests in property of the Government of Haiti and the de facto regime in Haiti that are in the United States or under the control of U.S. persons. It also blocks property of certain Haitian nationals who give substantial support to, or do substantial business with, the de facto regime, as identified by the Secretary of the Treasury. The order prohibits U.S. persons from selling or shipping petroleum, petroleum products, arms, and related materiel to Haiti, and it bars transactions that evade these rules. It also revokes parts of earlier Haiti orders to the extent they conflict with this order.

12846.s: This order blocks property and interests in property of certain commercial, industrial, and public utility entities organized or located in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) that are in the United States or under control of U.S. persons. It also allows vessels, freight vehicles, rolling stock, aircraft, and cargo suspected of violating certain U.N. resolutions to be detained and then blocked if a violation is found. U.S.-registered or U.S.-owned vessels may not enter the territorial waters of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and U.S. persons are prohibited from dealing with imports, exports, or transshipment through certain protected or controlled areas in Croatia and Bosnia-Hercegovina.

12775.s: This order declares a national emergency over events in Haiti and blocks property and interests in property of the Government of Haiti and its agencies that are in the United States or under control of United States persons. It also prohibits direct or indirect payments or transfers to the de facto regime in Haiti by United States persons or by Haitian entities owned or controlled by United States persons. Transfers or payments owed to the Government of Haiti must be made into an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York or as directed by the Secretary of the Treasury. The order does not block private Haitian assets subject to United States jurisdiction or stop remittances to Haitian persons other than the de facto regime in Haiti.

12722.s: This order blocks property and interests in property of the Government of Iraq, its agencies, controlled entities, and the Central Bank of Iraq that are in the United States or under the control of U.S. persons. It also prohibits many transactions with Iraq, including imports from Iraq, exports to Iraq, transportation and travel-related transactions, contracts in Iraq, and new credits or loans to the Iraqi government and related entities. The order applies to U.S. persons and took effect immediately.

12561.s: This order gives the Secretary of State the President’s authority to set maximum per diem allowances and reimbursements for official travel expenses for government employees in places outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, and U.S. possessions. It also covers localities in Alaska and Hawaii for that travel authority. The order changes a prior executive order and revokes Executive Order 11294.

12532.s: This order declares a national emergency over the South African government’s policies and sets limits on trade and other dealings with South Africa. It blocks certain loans, computer exports for use by South African government and security entities, some nuclear-related exports and approvals, and imports of South African arms, ammunition, military vehicles, and related data. It also urges U.S. firms and U.S. agencies working in South Africa to follow fair labor principles, and it directs steps on scholarships, human rights funding, and a study on Krugerrands.

12434.s: This order gives the Secretary of Transportation authority to operate and administer the Alaska Railroad. It says the Secretary may set and change passenger and freight rates, but those rates are subject to the Interstate Commerce Commission. The order also allows rate contracts to be filed with the Commission, lets other shippers seek similar contract rates under similar conditions, and supersedes Executive Order 11107.

12507.s: This order changes the rule for the President's Commission on Organized Crime. It says the commission will end on April 1, 1986, or thirty days after it submits its final report, whichever comes first.

12324.s: This order directs the State Department to make arrangements with foreign governments to prevent illegal migration to the United States by sea. It tells the Coast Guard to stop and board certain vessels outside U.S. territorial waters, check documents, and return vessels and passengers to the country they came from when there is reason to believe immigration laws are being broken. It says refugees cannot be returned without their consent. It also directs the Attorney General to help ensure fair enforcement of immigration laws and to observe international obligations for people who flee persecution.

12283.s: This order directs the Treasury Secretary to issue rules blocking claims against the Government of Iran tied to the hostage seizure, the hostages' detention, damage in the U.S. Embassy compound in Tehran, and certain injuries to U.S. nationals or their property. It also stops any court cases based on those claims and bars enforcement of court orders in those cases. The Attorney General is directed to notify courts that the litigation has ended.

12278.s: This order directs certain U.S. banks and banking institutions to transfer Iranian government funds, securities, and deposits held overseas to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, to be handled as the Secretary of the Treasury directs. It also cancels certain set-offs against those Iranian assets and revokes licenses and authorizations to claim or attach them. People subject to U.S. jurisdiction are barred from using court orders or similar actions to get rights in those assets.

12170.s: This order declares a national emergency over the situation in Iran. It blocks all property and interests in property of the Government of Iran, its controlled entities, and the Central Bank of Iran that are subject to U.S. jurisdiction or held by people subject to U.S. jurisdiction. It also authorizes the Secretary of the Treasury to use powers under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to carry it out.

12164.s: This order changes a prior executive order on multilateral development institutions. It adds the Director of the International Development Cooperation Agency to the groups and officials covered by that order. It also says the Director shall advise the Secretary of the Treasury and U.S. representatives to several international development banks and funds on the development aspects of matters related to those institutions. The order takes effect on October 1, 1979.

12131.s: This order establishes the President's Export Council and expands its membership to include executive agency heads, members of Congress, and up to 28 presidentially appointed citizens. The Council serves as a national advisory body on U.S. export trade and advises on plans and actions that affect export expansion. It may also create subordinate committees, and the Secretary of Commerce provides support for its work.

12047.s: This order gives the Director of the International Communication Agency the President’s role under the 1965 act for imported works of art and other objects of cultural significance. The Director may decide whether an object is of cultural significance and whether its temporary exhibition or display in the United States is in the national interest, and must publish public notices in the Federal Register. The Director must consult with the Secretary of State on national interest, may consult other government officials on cultural significance, and may delegate these functions within the Agency. It also revokes Executive Order 11312, while actions already in effect under that order stay in place until changed.

11989.s: This order amends a prior executive order on off-road vehicles on public lands. It lets agency heads close areas or trails to off-road vehicles if they cause or are causing harm to soil, vegetation, wildlife, wildlife habitat, or cultural or historic resources. It also allows agencies to close public lands to off-road vehicles except for areas or trails that are specifically designated as open.

11923.s: The order directs that the U.S. flag be flown at half-staff on June 21, 1976. This applies to federal buildings, grounds, and naval vessels in the United States and its territories and possessions. It also applies to U.S. embassies, consular offices, other facilities abroad, and military facilities and naval vessels and stations.

11841.s: This order adds a Development Coordination Committee to the foreign assistance rules. The committee includes officials from several departments and agencies, and its chairman may consult other federal agencies on matters within its work. Under the Secretary of State’s foreign policy guidance, the committee advises the President on coordinating U.S. policies and programs that affect the development of developing countries, including bilateral and multilateral development assistance.

11801.s: This order directs that the U.S. flag be flown at half-staff on the day of interment as a mark of respect for Ambassador Rodger P. Davies, who was killed while carrying out his duty. It applies to Federal Government buildings, grounds, and naval vessels in the District of Columbia, across the United States, and in its territories and possessions. It also applies at U.S. embassies, consular offices, and other facilities abroad, including military facilities and naval vessels and stations.

11686.s: This order carries out the Federal Advisory Committee Act and tells executive departments and agencies to take action to comply with it. It also gives the Director of the Office of Management and Budget certain duties, including preparing annual reports to Congress and setting guidelines and controls for advisory committees. The order revokes one part of Executive Order 11671 and says the rest of that order is superseded after ninety days.

11593.s: This order tells federal agencies to help preserve, restore, and maintain the Nation’s historic and cultural places. Agencies must identify and nominate qualifying federally owned sites, buildings, districts, and objects for the National Register of Historic Places, and use caution before transferring, selling, demolishing, or greatly changing them. It also requires agencies to make records of listed properties if they are to be altered or demolished, and to work with buyers or transferees on plans that fit preservation goals. The Secretary of the Interior must help develop the rules, advise agencies, and review related procedures and plans.

11408.s: This order revokes Executive Order No. 9, which dealt with dual Federal-State office holding, and Executive Order No. 9367, which barred Government employees from instructing people for certain Government examinations. It also revokes prior executive orders that interpreted or amended Executive Order No. 9. The changes affect Federal rules on office holding and on Government employees giving exam instruction.

11348.s: This order directs the Government to develop employee training programs to improve public service, efficiency, and the use of modern practices. It gives the Civil Service Commission a lead role in planning, promoting, and coordinating training, and it tells agency heads to manage training programs in their agencies. It also allows agencies to use interagency training and non-Government training resources, and it revokes Executive Order 10800.

11287.s: This order sets rules for awarding the National Medal of Science to people who have made outstanding contributions in the physical, biological, mathematical, or engineering sciences. It limits the award to no more than twenty people each year and says the recipient must be a U.S. citizen or national, or a lawful permanent resident who has filed for naturalization and is not permanently barred from citizenship. It also creates a President’s Committee to help review recommendations and send them to the President.

11215.s: This order creates the President's Commission on the Patent System. The commission is made up of certain federal officials and up to ten other members chosen by the President, and it may also have observers from the Department of State and the Office of Science and Technology. It must study the patent system, look for needed changes, and recommend improvements and any needed legislation. The commission must send a preliminary report and a final report to the President, and it revokes Executive Order No. 8977.

10665.s: This order restores a 5.05-acre parcel of the Schofield Barracks Military Reservation on Oahu to the possession, use, and control of the Territory of Hawaii. The land is to be used for National Guard purposes only unless the Department of the Army allows other uses. It also keeps a power line easement on the land and says the land will revert to Army control if it is used for other purposes and that use continues after notice to stop.

9374.s: This order transfers Lieutenant Daniel E. Whelan, Jr. from the Coast and Geodetic Survey to the Navy Department. While under Navy Department control, he serves under his Coast and Geodetic Survey commission and is part of the active naval forces of the United States. He is to be returned to the Coast and Geodetic Survey when the present national emergency ends. Commander Henry B. Campbell is also returned to the Coast and Geodetic Survey.

6023.s: This order designates the air space over the District of Columbia as a prohibited area from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. on March 4, 1933, for public-safety purposes. During that time, no aircraft may fly through that air space unless the Secretary of Commerce specifically permits it.

u-cleveland2-18970102.s: The order changes Civil Service Rule VIII so a vacancy may be filled without examination and certification when there are no eligible names on the register and the public interest requires it, if the Commission approves. These temporary appointments end when an eligible is provided, and no person may serve longer than three months in any one year unless the Commission gives special authority first. It also allows a vacancy to be filled without following the rule for up to thirty days in an emergency while a certificate is issued and the appointment is completed.

u-bharrison-18930118.s: This order announces the death of Rutherford B. Hayes, who served as President of the United States from March 4, 1877, to March 4, 1881. It orders the Executive Mansion and the executive departments at Washington to be draped in mourning and the flags there to be at half-staff for thirty days. It also suspends public business in the departments on the day of the funeral and calls for suitable military and naval honors.

u-cleveland1-18861118-2.s: This order directs the Navy to lower the ensign at each naval station and on each United States Navy vessel in commission to half-mast on the day of the funeral, or the day after receipt if it arrives too late. It also directs that a gun be fired every half hour from sunrise to sunset at each naval station and on board flagships and vessels acting singly. Officers of the Navy and Marine Corps are to wear the usual badge of mourning for a period of thirty days.
